full_text:
Jim Harbaugh (left), Justin Herbert (No. 10) and Mike McDaniel left plenty to second-guess in Sunday's loss to the Cardinals. Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
Two NFL head coaches made bold proclamations heading into the 2026 season.
One of them looks smarter than the other today.
Ben Johnson said his Chicago Bears hoped to average 38 points per game , enough to set a single-season scoring record. Jim Harbaugh said his Los Angeles Chargers quarterback, Justin Herbert, would go down as the greatest in league history .
After Johnson’s Bears ran all over Carolina’s defense during a 59-37 victory, Harbaugh’s Chargers fell 26-14 at home to the Arizona Cardinals , who entered Week 1 as the heaviest underdog (+10.5) by far.
The first Pick Six column of this new season leads with an analysis of the Chargers’ dispiriting opener and a look at why Herbert won’t become the best QB in franchise history, let alone the league.
We’ll also run through how all the new offensive play callers fared, from the Chargers’ Mike McDaniel to Baltimore’s Declan Doyle (41 points!) and Cleveland’s Todd Monken (49 plays!). We’ll include Buffalo’s Joe Brady (409 yards against Houston’s defense!) now that he’s calling plays as a head coach for the first time. The full menu:
• About that Herbert GOAT talk • Doyle, Monken and new callers • Rams, Panthers paid for this? • Why Rams should be concerned • Stroud, Young and second deals • Two-minute drill: Cards and Vikes
A defensive coach who has faced Herbert multiple times compares and contrasts the Chargers’ quarterback to Josh Allen.
Both are a tick slower than most top quarterbacks at seeing the game and processing it, this coach said. That gives defenses a chance to counter their superior athletic and throwing ability. The way the defensive coach sees things, Allen has been in the same offense long enough to improve his processing (this is his fourth season with Brady calling plays). That has helped him ascend. Herbert, in contrast, is on his fifth offensive coordinator in seven NFL seasons.
“I still like the guy and think he’s good,” this defensive coach said of Herbert. “But if he does have a little success, Mike (McDaniel) will get a new job as a head coach. He just has to have a decent year, and the cycle will continue for the quarterback.”
Both the Bills and Chargers have invested resources into building strong offensive lines for their quarterbacks. While Buffalo has succeeded, the Chargers have struggled. Injuries at tackle wiped out their line last season. Weakness on the interior figures to be a problem this season, giving Herbert less time to process.
Sunday’s first impression was not encouraging, as the Chargers managed just 14 points and 268 yards against a defense that finished 28th in EPA per play last season. The chest injury that knocked top receiver Ladd McConkey from the game in the third quarter marked a turning point. The Chargers averaged 6.3 yards on the 26 plays with McConkey on the field but only 4.2 across the 25 plays without him. Herbert’s EPA per pass play plummeted from +0.22 to -0.33.
As for Harbaugh, he’ll remain the ultimate cheerleader for his quarterback.
“Justin Herbert, when it’s all said and done, when his career comes to an end, I predict he will be known as the greatest, best ever to play the position of quarterback,” Harbaugh said heading into this season.
The comment recalled what Harbaugh said in 2011 about Alex Smith, then his quarterback with the 49ers.
“He’s every bit the elite quarterback as there is playing in the game right now,” Harbaugh said then.
Smith had tossed 10 touchdowns while going 7-1 as a starter under Harbaugh to that point, ranking 21st in EPA per pass play. Aaron Rodgers had 24 touchdown passes over the same period. Drew Brees had 21. Tom Brady had 20. Smith was not nearly as elite as those guys, but Harbaugh didn’t care.
The interesting thing about Herbert is not whether he’ll go down as the “greatest, best ever” quarterback in league history. That isn’t happening. The interesting part is whether Herbert can make anything close to the jump his long-ago Hall of Fame Chargers predecessor, Dan Fouts, made at the same point in his career.
Fouts, like Herbert, was solid but unspectacular for the Chargers during his first six NFL seasons.
Fouts ranked fifth in yards per attempt and 12th in passer rating among 24 quarterbacks with at least 40 starts over his first six seasons, commanding zero MVP votes. His career trajectory changed when Don Coryell took over as the Chargers' head coach entering his seventh season. Fouts then ranked first in yards per attempt and second to Joe Montana in passer rating over the next six seasons. He was named first-team All-Pro twice and finished among the top six in MVP voting four times.
Herbert will never play for Coryell, who was elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame posthumously in 2023. He is getting to play for the only coach since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger to score 70 points in a game. But McDaniel probably won't be with the Chargers for the long term, and the Chargers' offensive depth is concerning, especially if McConkey misses time.
Harbaugh has been at his best when able to assemble an all-star staff. He sets the tone but isn't a differentiating offensive designer able to elevate an offense by himself. Longer term, Herbert might need the Chargers to hire the next Coryell, not the next Harbaugh.
It was only one week. It must be better next week against the Raiders, ahead of a seven-game stretch against the Bills, Seahawks, Broncos, Chiefs, Rams, Texans and Ravens, with five of those on the road.
"They are going to have their hands full with the Raiders next week," another coach said, "because the Raiders are organized, they have a veteran quarterback and their defensive front is decent."
NFL offenses averaged more than 24 points per game in Week 1, which would be the highest for an opening week this century if it holds through Monday night. Teams were under center on early downs 50.4 percent of the time, the highest rate for any week since the 2017 season. The final week of the 2025 season ranks second at 47.1 percent, affirming a trend that is helping offenses present a run threat more convincingly.
Coaches can be quick to offer theories as to why. The absence of offseason tackling and preseason reps rank high on their list, but those aren't new developments. A quick look at preseason playing time over the past eight seasons showed no correlation.
And so we'll give some of these offenses their due. The jobs Arizona's Mike LaFleur, Las Vegas' Klint Kubiak and the New York Jets' Frank Reich executed Sunday stand apart because those three offensive play callers revived units that ranked 21st (Cardinals), 29th (Jets) and 31st (Raiders) in EPA per play last season. And all three won.
We begin with the offensive play callers burdened not by their teams' recent struggles, but rather those leading offenses where good might not be good enough. Brady, the Bills' offensive play caller since 2023, makes the list because this is his first season calling plays without having to run the game plan past the head coach.
Joe Brady, Bills: Allen's numbers in two games against Houston over the past two seasons were far worse than they were against seven other opponents he faced more than once over that span. His passer rating (62.2), yards per attempt (6.0), completion percentage (51.6) and EPA per pass play (-0.11) in those two losses at Houston were all evidence that the Texans' defense was on the verge of becoming legendary .
This Bills performance ranks No. 1 against the Texans in 39 total games over the past three seasons by points scored (36), EPA per play (0.28), yards per play (8.1) and yards per pass attempt (11.5). It validated the Bills' standing as the No. 1 team in the AFC, as projected by league executives heading into the season. Big relief for Bills fans.

title: How the Bills unleashed Dalton Kincaid against Texans: 7 Week 1 observations Dalton Kincaid starred as the Bills leaned on tight ends against Houston. Plus, Jim Leonhard’s debut, James Cook’s role and more. Joe Buscaglia 32

full_text:
Buffalo Bills tight end Dalton Kincaid had five catches for 130 yards total — the most for any tight end in franchise history since 1967. David Buono / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
For the first time in Josh Allen’s career, he leaves Houston a winner.
The Bills’ 36-31 shootout win gave us our first chance to see how all of Buffalo’s new variables melded together on the field.
With a new head coach, new defensive coordinator and defensive scheme, a new No. 1 receiver, and new starters at nearly half the defensive positions, there was a lot to glean from the Week 1 showdown.
It begins with arguably Sunday’s biggest development — something the Bills have been waiting almost two full years to see.
The Bills entered the game knowing they needed to have a plan for Houston’s edge-rushing duo of Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter. The pressure and sacks the Bills allowed the Texans in their 2025 matchup simply could not happen again, which meant they needed a different philosophical approach.
In his first game as both offensive play caller and head coach, Joe Brady made packages with multiple tight ends the star of the show. Including penalties, the Bills wound up with 56 total plays, and they used at least two tight ends on 29 of those, an astounding 51.8 percent. Their commitment to 13 personnel — three tight ends — was even more striking: The Bills used that grouping on 20 of their 56 plays, or 35.7 percent.
For context, that 13 personnel usage more than doubled any Bills single-game rate since they drafted Allen in 2018. The previous high in one game for 13 personnel over the last three years was only 16 percent, according to TruMedia.
They felt empowered to use 13 personnel for one distinct reason: They wanted to unleash a fully healthy Dalton Kincaid as the cheat code to the matchup. By using so many tight ends at once, the Bills forced the Texans to keep heavier players on the field. However, Kincaid looked legitimately different than he had at any point since late 2024. The player who flashed so much potential in the second half of his rookie season in 2023 was back.
Even on simple motion in the backfield, his acceleration was eye-opening. He can challenge defenses at the intermediate and deep levels and make difficult catches look easy. A player that size, with that speed and receiving ability, is a potential matchup nightmare for opposing teams when he’s fully healthy.
We clearly saw how that could play out against the Texans, one of the best defenses in the league. Three of Kincaid’s receptions went for at least 35 yards. Two of those came with the Bills in 13 personnel, furthering their advantage from that grouping. He had five catches for 130 yards total — the most for any Bills tight end since 1967. But his game was so much more than just those five plays. What we saw is the vision the Bills have clung to since his injury woes began, and why they kept standing by him.
It wasn’t just the 13 personnel usage with Kincaid; it was the overall role. By my unofficial count, Kincaid was on the field for 73 percent of the Bills’ offensive plays, the most of any Bills tight end. It is the highest snap share Kincaid has had since Nov. 3, 2024 — the game before he suffered a PCL injury to his knee that bogged him down for almost two years. After his injury in 2024, Kincaid took only 37 percent of snaps in games played the rest of the season. In 2025, Kincaid managed only 39 percent of snaps in games all season.
The Bills teased this type of usage during training camp practices and delivered on it, and in turn, Kincaid delivered the breakout performance of his career. His performance yielded an astonishing 5.65 yards per route run. That would have ranked 12th among all NFL single-game performances in 2025 by players who ran at least 20 routes.
If Kincaid can stay healthy — which is a big ‘if’ given his history — he and No. 1 receiver DJ Moore suddenly change the entire complexion of the Bills offense in 2026.
The first go-round for new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard didn’t go as well as he hoped. While the Bills bookended their day with turnovers off Greg Rousseau strip-sacks, much of the game was marred by inconsistency, chunk plays and question marks against an average Texans offense. The Bills had a tough time on third and fourth downs, allowing the Texans to convert on 55 percent of opportunities — penalties included.
Leonhard has the mind for the role and the potential to be a very good defensive coordinator, but the Bills looked like a team with a bunch of new defensive starters in their first real game with a new defensive scheme.
The flashes are what the Bills will keep coming back to, but they’ve got some real question marks at cornerback, inside linebacker, on dime looks, and in generating consistent pressure throughout the game.
Until the Bills settle into Leonhard’s scheme, their defense could remain inconsistent from series to series, setting the stage for more early-season shootouts.
Without Ty Johnson available due to a hamstring injury, the Bills smartly wanted to see if their top rusher, James Cook, could stay on the field for third downs. The Bills kept Cook on the field for three late-down situations — two on third down and one on fourth down.
That came to a screeching halt in the second half. The Bills didn’t use Cook on a third down the rest of the game, instead going with practice squad call-up Frank Gore Jr. on six of the seven third-down chances in the second half. Ray Davis had the other third-down snap in the second half.
The Bills were open to the idea of using a platoon at the second cornerback spot, and they delivered on doing that — but not to a grand degree. Starter Maxwell Hairston came off the field for only two defensive series, with rookie Davison Igbinosun getting the chance on those.
Igbinosun made it through his first full series with both a holding penalty and a pass breakup. On his second, the Bills pulled him mid-series after a 21-yard Kayshon Boutte catch. Hairston wound up with 71 of the 81 possible plays against the Texans.
If one thing was clear with Leonhard, it’s that he wanted his best defensive front players (defensive line and outside linebackers) in the game as much as possible. That was led by defensive lineman Ed Oliver, who was unofficially on the field for 82.7 percent of the Bills’ defensive plays (penalties included). Outside linebackers Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb weren’t far behind at 80.3 percent each.
Second-year defensive lineman Landon Jackson has had a positive summer leading up to the season and moved up the depth chart as a result.
That, along with T.J. Sanders’ injury, set the table for him to have an enhanced role on Sunday, but the Bills didn’t veer from one personnel grouping for Jackson. On all 30 of his snaps, Jackson lined up at defensive end in a base defense look with two other defensive linemen with him.
He didn’t take a single snap as one of only two defensive linemen. It could come in the future, but they kept things simple for Jackson in Week 1.
The Bills used a pretty specific third-down grouping for most of the game. They deviated a couple of times for a different look, but the group mostly consisted of the same players and substitutions.
They would take out defensive lineman Deone Walker and replace him with outside linebacker Michael Hoecht as an interior rusher, leaving Oliver as the only defensive lineman.
Then, they substituted safety Damar Hamlin for inside linebacker Dorian Williams, put Hamlin at safety, and had starting safety Cole Bishop line up in the box next to inside linebacker Terrel Bernard. Given their late-down struggles, the Bills may need to switch things up if it continues.
Up Next: The Bills head home on a short week to take on the 1-0 Detroit Lions on Thursday night — the regular-season debut of their new $2.2 billion stadium.

full_text:
Neither C.J. Stroud, left, nor Bryce Young got a contract extension before starting their fourth NFL season. Tim Warner / Getty Images
( Editor’s note: This is excerpted from Mike Sando’s Pick Six of Sept. 14, 2026.)
Houston’s C.J. Stroud and Carolina’s Bryce Young combined for five touchdown passes while quarterbacking Week 1 offenses that topped 30 points. Both lost against 2025 playoff teams led by quarterbacks with Tier 1 credentials (Josh Allen, who led Buffalo at Houston, 36-31) or Tier 1 potential (Caleb Williams, who led Chicago to a 59-37 victory at Carolina).
The obvious differences between Allen/Williams and Stroud/Young should make any team pause before entering into a top-of-market deal with a mid-tier quarterback.
Stroud’s production to this point in his career includes a No. 20 ranking in EPA per pass play, about the same as the rankings for Trevor Lawrence (21st) and Kyler Murray (22nd) when those players signed top-of-market extensions with Jacksonville and Arizona, respectively.
Young’s No. 34 ranking in EPA per pass play since entering the league tracks with the No. 33 ranking for Daniel Jones when Jones re-signed with the Giants. Young has been trending positively, but he still ranks only 25th among 32 qualifying quarterbacks since the start of last season (Stroud ranks 14th on that list).
The chart above stacks 10 quarterbacks drafted in the first round from 2018-23 by how quickly they received second contracts. Lawrence, Murray, Allen and Joe Burrow signed new deals after three seasons, the earliest allowed under labor rules. Jones and Tagovailoa waited as questions about their abilities lingered. Lamar Jackson's situation was a one-off in that he was a former MVP operating without an agent, which complicated negotiations.
The bottom line: Teams with significant questions about their quarterbacks through three seasons — the Giants with Jones, the Dolphins with Tagovailoa — regretted those decisions enough for others to preserve their flexibility.

summary:

full_text:
Caleb Williams is the top-scoring fantasy quarterback of Week 1 after Sunday's slate. Jared C. Tilton / Getty Images
With four minutes of game clock remaining in Carolina on Sunday, the Bears and Panthers had already combined for the highest point total of any season-opener in NFL history. The teams had gained over 900 total yards. Unsurprisingly, they were not finished scoring.
D’Andre Swift punctuated Chicago’s 59-37 win with a late 28-yard score, his third rushing touchdown of the game. Swift and Kyle Monangai each topped 100 rushing yards, and the Bears had delivered 552 net yards of offense. Carolina had gained 478, which would be more than enough most weeks.
Chicago’s Caleb Williams was the top-scoring fantasy quarterback Sunday, and Carolina’s Bryce Young ranked third, just behind Buffalo’s Josh Allen. Williams, in fact, had produced one of the greatest quarterback performances in recent Bears history:
Caleb Williams with the best performance for a Bears QB in a season opener since at least 2000 by passer rating (124.1), completion percentage (72.4%) and EPA per dropback (0.48) per @TruMediaSports .
— Kevin Fishbain (@kfishbain) September 13, 2026
He cooked the Panthers for 269 yards and two scores, rushing for 65 and two more. Just look at this filthy throw to Cole Kmet:
CHIvsCAR on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/KedXXw4da5
— NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026
Williams played every quarter on Sunday like he played fourth quarters last year. All that preseason talk about his development and next-level command of the offense seems legit.
You might naturally assume that on a day in which the Bears offense was shattering records, tight end Colston Loveland and wideouts Luther Burden and/or Rome Odunze would have feasted. But you’d be wrong. Instead, new arrival WR Kalif Raymond led the team in receiving (8 receptions, 84 yards), and Loveland was shut out.
A quiet week from three premier receiving threats isn’t much of a concern, however, because, again: Chicago just hung 59 points and 552 yards on an opponent. Loveland will have better days. Everyone will eat. Any skill player tied to Ben Johnson’s offense is a potential matchup-winner in any given week. Good, better, best , things of that nature. The Bears are gonna be a wagon.
Another reason to feel supreme confidence in this team’s juggernaut potential is that Chicago’s defense appears to be just as hideous as the fantasy community had hoped. This was a unit that hemorrhaged yards last season, relying on takeaways to an unreasonable extent. The personnel did not obviously improve in the offseason and All-Pro safety Kevin Byard relocated in free agency. The Bears simply had no answers for WRs Jalen Coker (8 receptions, 138 yards, 2 TDs) or Tetairoa McMillan (5 receptions, 75 yards) on Sunday, plus they allowed RB Chuba Hubbard to erupt for 87 total yards and two scores. Carolina receivers were separating with hilarious ease.
Full credit to Coker, an excellent player and multi-year fantasy sleeper, but Chicago’s secondary just made him look like 6-foot-3 Steve Smith. Coker definitely won’t be the only receiver to clear 30 fantasy points against the Bears this season. We’ll be picking on this defense all year. Minnesota’s WRs Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison should detonate next week.
Essentially, we have a perfect fantasy storm in Chicago. An inventive offense loaded with playmakers, paired with an undertalented turnstile defense. We cannot rule out the possibility that this team will average 30+ points per game offensively while giving up nearly as many.
We’d recommend bookmarking the Bears schedule to assist with weekly waiver plans. This team is about to take us on the wildest ride.
Statistically, New Orleans’ RB Etienne had a perfectly acceptable day by his standards, finishing with 78 scrimmage yards on 16 touches, with seven receptions included. A fine PPR effort. It’s the sort of stat line you can take to the trade market, in fact.
And, um … maybe you should consider doing just that, because Etienne was something less than a full-timer in the Saints’ OT loss to Detroit. He played only 53 of 90 total snaps. Kendre Miller scored the lone rushing touchdown for New Orleans while handling as many carries as Etienne (9). Their touches and snap counts were nearly even at halftime.
Etienne still held a massive edge in routes and targets, as you’d expect in a game in which his team once trailed 21-0. Still, the Saints backfield was an unmistakable committee. It’s particularly concerning when we consider that Alvin Kamara was out of the mix in the season-opener. Sunday’s usage was supposed to represent something close to Etienne’s top-end potential.
The good news, of course, is that New Orleans put 30 points on the board despite sleepwalking for half the game. If the offense exceeds expectations, Etienne can justify his draft price on a less-than-ideal workload. He’s on the list of things worth worrying about, however.
It’s never a huge surprise to see Buffalo’s Kincaid make a field-flipping splash play, as happened multiple times on Sunday at Houston:
Josh Allen with the throw and Dalton Kincaid with the catch
BUFvsHOU on CBS/Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/fj7tVqbYlg
— NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026
Kincaid is a known commodity as a receiver. The holes in his game have been playing time and availability. Kincaid didn’t play more than 55% of the offensive snaps in any game last season. He’s also missed nine games over the past two years, sidelined by injuries.
Against the Texans, however, he rarely came off the field. Kincaid played 73.7% of the snaps for Buffalo and finished as the team’s leading receiver (5 receptions, 130 yards). The Bills don’t get that road win without him.
Nothing about Sunday’s performance guarantees that Kincaid can remain healthy over the full season, obviously, but his usage was exactly what we like to see. If it holds, he’s a potential top-five player at his position. We don’t see many big-play tight ends, but Kincaid is clearly one of them.
As a prospect, the Commanders’ Williams was praised by scouts for his hands and ball-skills, and, well … credit to the scouts. They seem to have nailed it. Williams was excellent in his regular season debut for Washington, catching four balls on as many targets for 64 yards and a stylish TD on an off-target throw:
The Commanders get the late TD
: FOX pic.twitter.com/2avBN9UFxU
— FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) September 13, 2026
Four targets won’t generally pay the fantasy bills, but Williams certainly made the most of them. He roasted the Eagles’ DB Cooper DeJean at least once. You’ll find Williams’ name in most waiver columns this week.
As for Miami’s Douglas, he continues to look like a future star. Possibly a current star. We might prefer to see him attached to a healthier offensive environment, sure, but Douglas can play . He delivered 94 of Malik Willis’ 220 passing yards, catching five balls on seven chances. Douglas should get rescued from waiver wires this week. He’s too good to remain unattached. He has ideal size (6-foot-4) and speed (4.39), plus he was a buzzy name throughout the summer. Go get him.
Look, you can’t simply give away your second-round pick after a single terrible game. Panic-trading won’t help you. Atlanta’s offense was tragically dysfunctional with a compromised version of Cooper Rush at quarterback. Twelve passes were completed by Rush, only two of which went to London. The team gained 238 total net yards and Bijan Robinson supplied 173 of them. Passing to anyone but Bijan proved hopeless. Ugly day.
We hate to tell you to pin all your hopes to the return of Michael Penix, but that’s where we’re at. Shrug . He could return as early as next week. London produced a 100-catch season just two years ago and Penix was involved. He cannot possibly be a downgrade from Rush. London made it through the Desmond Ridder era, so he can overcome this current mess. He’s also headed into a matchup with a Panthers…

full_text:
D'Andre Swift led a powerful Bears ground attack on Sunday, rushing for 124 yards and three touchdowns. David Jensen / Getty Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Leave it to Chicago Bears coach Ben Johnson to make the understatement of the week when talking about his running back, D’Andre Swift.
“He’s had a good week, huh?” Johnson said, almost offering the slightest of smiles after the Bears’ jaw-dropping 59-37 victory over the Carolina Panthers in Sunday’s season opener.
Swift, who signed a three-year contract extension Saturday morning, rushed for 124 yards and three touchdowns, earning a game ball.
The soft-spoken back said to his teammates in the postgame locker-room celebration, “We work too hard. Let the work show week in and week out. Proud of y’all.”
No one who works for the Bears would have worried that Swift would be any different after a payday. But for him to put together a performance like that immediately after cashing in, it served as a reminder of what he stands for, and why general manager Ryan Poles rewarded him.
“That’s always my mindset,” Swift said. “I feel like I’m just getting started, man. I was just grateful to be able to keep going with these guys. My mindset wasn’t gonna change whether it was something done or not, know what I mean? I got something to prove every day I wake up.”
He proved it by being part of Bears history — Swift accounted for only half of the Bears’ six rushing touchdowns, along with two by quarterback Caleb Williams and one from running back Kyle Monangai. It was the Bears’ most rushing scores in a game since 1941.
The 2026 season began with a 17-yard Swift run wiped out by a holding penalty on wide receiver Rome Odunze. When the Bears got the ball back after the Panthers jumped out to a 7-0 lead, cashing in on Luther Burden’s fumble, Johnson put the ball back in Swift’s hands.
On first-and-10 from the Panthers’ 45-yard line, Swift took a handoff and followed his blocker to the right side of the line. Tight end Cole Kmet had a powerful block coming from his fullback position and right guard Jonah Jackson sealed his man. Once Swift got through the line, he spun off a tackle attempt from Panthers corner Will Lee, juked to his left and cut back across the field to avoid more Panthers defensive backs. The 32-yard run was his longest of the day and set up Williams’ 9-yard touchdown.
“Good blocking up front,” Swift said. “(My) mentality — wasn’t trying to go down by any means.”
Swift’s first two touchdowns, both 1-yard plunges, looked easy. The offensive line was moving Panthers defenders, and he charged into the end zone.
Swift’s 124 yards are the second most for a Bears running back in a season opener this century, trailing Matt Forte’s 141 from 2015. The team’s 291 yards rushing marked its highest total in any game since 1984.
Williams paused after receiving the question because he wanted to use the exact right words to describe his running back.
“He’s a golden star. Because he can do everything,” Williams said. “He can catch, he can block. Obviously he can run downhill, he runs wide zone, he can run tosses … get on the edge and from there he’s not only just getting first downs, he’s trying to take them to the crib. He’s a special player and happy that we got him for the next three, four years.”
Said guard Jonah Jackson, “D’Andre is awesome, man. He’s a Philly cat who has some piss and vinegar to him. He can go side to side with the best of ’em. But you better believe he can get it going downhill.”
After watching his backfield mate, Monangai, take a handoff and go 61 yards for a touchdown, Swift got one more carry, and he sealed the win with a 28-yard touchdown run, the Bears’ final points.
“I mean, he earned it, every step of it,” Johnson said. “We really value what he brings to the table. He’s had a great spring, a great training camp, and so I don’t think anybody in our building is surprised that he’s out of the gate in a strong fashion.”
Last year, Swift and Monangai became the first Bears duo of backs since Walter Payton and Matt Suhey in 1985 to rush for 100 yards in the same game when they did it on Black Friday, the signature win in Philadelphia. They did it again Sunday against the Panthers while also getting 65 yards from Williams. In that win over the Eagles, Williams had only 13 rushing yards.
Swift’s three touchdown runs are a franchise best in a season opener this century. His connection with his head coach continues to grow, and a coach who loves to bludgeon an opponent with the run game got to do so to kick off the season.
“I take a lot of pride in making sure my coaches are able to trust me when I’m out there,” Swift said. “So I don’t take nothing for granted. Every single day I wake up, I have something to prove going into the building and even more so now, it’s a lot on my shoulders as far as I need to deliver when my number is called, and that’s what I look forward to doing every time.”
In 2024, Swift joined the Bears as a free agent whose production didn’t match the contract in a rough year overall for the offense. In fact, many wondered if the Bears would look to replace him in Johnson’s first season.
Instead, Swift had a career year, followed it up with an eye-opening training camp, earned a contract extension — which is still rare for his position — and then responded to it all with three trips to the end zone in a Week 1 win.
The trust between coach and running back has never been stronger.
“(Johnson) knows every time I touch the ball,” Swift said, “I’m looking to score.”

summary:

JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — How much longer? How much longer will the Browns ask everyone else to pay the price for their Deshaun Watson debacle?
Jimmy Haslam’s name might be on the checks, but the list of people stuck paying the bill for the worst trade in franchise history continues to grow.
Watson was terrible again Sunday in the
full_text:
Deshaun Watson calls the signals during the fourth quarter of the Browns' 34-10 season-opening loss against the Jaguars in Jacksonville, Fla. Don Juan Moore / Getty Images
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — How much longer? How much longer will the Browns ask everyone else to pay the price for their Deshaun Watson debacle?
Jimmy Haslam’s name might be on the checks, but the list of people stuck paying the bill for the worst trade in franchise history continues to grow.
Watson was terrible again Sunday in the Browns’ 34-10 opening loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars because he’s been terrible for most of the last four years. Expecting that to magically transform now after two Achilles surgeries stacked on top of his already deep medical history and nearly 700 days away from the field was always naive at best and far closer to foolish for a franchise that knows a thing or six about foolish behavior.
Watson is no longer a good quarterback. Hasn’t been for years. He couldn’t get to the proper pocket depth when we last saw him on the field two years ago, so it shouldn’t have been surprising that he couldn’t do it again Sunday.
The interception on the opening drive was abysmal. The constant delay-of-game calls, false starts and inability to get lined up are a special level of alarming for a quarterback who entered the NFL 10 years ago. This isn’t a rookie or even a second-year guy. Watson is a decade into this league — and quickly playing his way out of it — making the same clumsy mistakes that plagued Shedeur Sanders as a late-round rookie last year.
The list of people forced to carry Watson’s burden in Cleveland is long and distinguished: Joe Flacco (the first time), Alex Van Pelt, Bill Callahan, Ken Dorsey, Kevin Stefanski and now Todd Monken.
All of them were saddled or scarred (sometimes both) while trying to make it work with the unworkable. Flacco couldn’t be brought back after too much success because the city actually liked him, and what would that mean for Deshaun?
Van Pelt was fired as offensive coordinator coming off a playoff appearance in a season the team cycled through five different starting quarterbacks. That firing was enough for Bill Callahan to see where everything was headed, and he slipped out the door to go coach with his son in Tennessee before this thing completely derailed. Which it now has.
Monken said throughout training camp this wasn’t a week-to-week audition for Watson, yet he wouldn’t commit to him for next week after just one game because how could he after watching that mess?
“It’s not just him,” Monken said. “We’re putting this on Deshaun, which is unfair.”
That’s what the head coach is expected to say, but anyone who watched the game and watched Watson’s previous 19 games in Cleveland knows it’s completely fair. He is where the bulk of the problems lie. His final numbers, 16 of 22, 205 yards, a touchdown and an interception, were heavily skewed by a late deep ball to Denzel Boston for a touchdown. Watson didn’t play nearly as well as the numbers indicated, and everyone with the Browns knows it.
Nobody can change what Watson has already cost them, regardless of how many times they keep trotting him back out there. But they can decide what he costs them next.
There’s legitimate reason for optimism with K.C. Concepcion, Denzel Boston and Harold Fannin, but it’s impossible to get a fair evaluation on them when the quarterback is dropping to 13 yards behind the line of scrimmage, holding onto the ball too long and consistently settling for check downs. The linemen can’t possibly set a proper pocket when they don’t know where the quarterback is setting up. These are the quarterbacking basics that were somehow erased from Watson’s factory settings before he arrived in Cleveland. He struggled with it two years ago when the Browns started 1-4, and he looked broken and disinterested before getting hurt.
The time away didn’t seem to make anything better.
A sunk cost drains budgets and rewires judgment. It convinces smart people that the money they’ve already spent is a reason to spend more rather than serving as the clearest argument to stop and walk away.
The money is gone, and it’s not coming back. The currency the Browns are dealing with now is time. Replacing the starter after one game would be outrageous for most franchises, but in this instance, the fact that Watson won the job at all is the outrageous part. The Browns once traded their starting quarterback, Charlie Frye, two days after a season opener, so what constitutes outrageous here is usually a bit different than everywhere else.
Monken is in this now. He had no ties to Watson and still chose to hook his reputation as a terrific offensive coach to the quarterback who has wrecked everything he has touched since landing here. Monken even sounded like Stefanski by the time the day was through, repeating things about it not being good enough and it being on all of them to fix it. Stefanski was skewered for similar coachspeak, but the part he couldn’t say out loud is the part you’re seeing now.
A lot of this isn’t fixable. At least not with Watson, and probably not with Sanders, either.
Running Watson out at quarterback next week at Tampa could be particularly embarrassing for Haslam after Baker Mayfield signed his mammoth extension with the Buccaneers last week. Mayfield isn’t elite, but he’s obviously been far better than what Watson has produced in Cleveland.
The meal is over at least for this week. The chicken was served raw and the vegetables were burned. Dessert was curdled and the drinks were flat. The whole thing was a bit of a mess, and Monken nevertheless is holding the check. He’s 60 years old, in his first year running an NFL operation, and spent the offseason talking about the identity he wanted his players to have. They showed none of it in their first opportunity.
It might be time to speak with a manager. The most important thing Monken can realize is this isn’t his mess. It’s not his bill to pay. Stop pretending like it is.

title: Cowboys' Week 1 disaster: Dak Prescott's costly mistake and defensive issues (again) Brian Schottenheimer said the Cowboys got "humbled" but they aren't pushing the panic button after the season-opening loss. Jon Machota 58
summary:
Dak Prescott had a costly first-half mistake and the Cowboys never recovered from it and lost their opener in New York. Elsa / Getty Images
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Jerry Jones acknowledged before the game that he was “anxious” and “nervous” about watching the Dallas Cowboys’ season opener against the New York Giants.
One of the last things he was probably concerned about was Dak Prescott. The franchise quarterback was part of the biggest play Sunday night at MetLife Stadium. It wasn’t a good one
full_text:
Dak Prescott had a costly first-half mistake and the Cowboys never recovered from it and lost their opener in New York. Elsa / Getty Images
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Jerry Jones acknowledged before the game that he was “anxious” and “nervous” about watching the Dallas Cowboys’ season opener against the New York Giants.
One of the last things he was probably concerned about was Dak Prescott. The franchise quarterback was part of the biggest play Sunday night at MetLife Stadium. It wasn’t a good one. His lone interception helped provide the Giants with a spark that eventually turned into a 28-20 Week 1 Cowboys loss .
“That was crucial,” Prescott said. “I was trying to throw the ball away. The guy made a hell of a play. I got to make sure that it’s out of bounds, though. I was surprised. It’s one I want back, obviously. I think that was a huge point in the game.”
Facing third-and-5 with just under a minute left in the second quarter and the score tied 7-7, Prescott was flushed out of the pocket, drifting 17 yards behind the line of scrimmage when he threw off his back foot.
Giants safety Jevon Holland made a sliding grab near the Cowboys sideline. New York scored six plays later, taking a 14-7 lead into the halftime locker room. The Giants then received the second-half kickoff and scored again 12 plays later.
“That was a big momentum swing,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said of the interception.
The Cowboys were never able to overcome that 21-7 deficit midway through the third quarter as they only had the ball for two possessions in the second half.
Aside from the turnover, Prescott didn’t have a bad game. The Giants displayed a strong pass rush, but he was never sacked. He was accurate most of the night, even when he wasn’t getting much help early from his top playmakers.
It was expected entering the season that with star wide receivers CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, Dallas would simply pick up where it left off a year ago as one of the NFL’s best offenses.
That didn’t happen Sunday night. Pickens had two costly drops in the first half, which was especially surprising because he was the Cowboys’ best training camp performer. He didn’t have two drops all of camp, but he had two on his first four targets against the Giants.
The Cowboys’ top two offensive weapons had only 27 receiving yards in the first half, with most of their big plays coming from drawing defensive pass interference calls. Pickens finished with only three catches for 28 yards. Lamb totaled five for 44 yards and a touchdown.
“It’ll get back to (clicking),” Prescott said. “Those guys had some uncharacteristic drops. I know that they’re upset about them immediately, came and made a comment about them and they moved on as they should. We’ll get back to it.”
If they don’t, the season could quickly become a repeat of a year ago, because the defense still has plenty of issues.
No one expected Christian Parker’s debut as defensive coordinator to go so poorly. Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart was outstanding, completing 23 of 29 passes for 230 yards and three touchdowns while also rushing for 54 yards on 11 carries.
He never seemed rushed in his decision-making as he constantly appeared to have all the answers to the test . That’s concerning because that was a major issue for the Cowboys a year ago under Matt Eberflus, far too often opposing quarterbacks would have a career day against Dallas.
“This defensive unit is really good,” Cowboys defensive tackle Quinnen Williams said. “We got the guys to be accountable and get better. … We can be better and we will be better.”
One of the biggest issues Sunday night was how easily the Giants were able to complete short passes into the flat for notable gains. That clearly bothered Schottenheimer.
“You got young players,” he said. “Young player closes and Jaxson Dart boots and gets outside. We don’t push three different times the f—ing flat route, excuse my language. Those are going to happen and we’re going to have to coach the young players better, but when you play young players, it’s part of the deal. And they need to learn quickly.”
Since trading Micah Parsons before the start of last season, the Cowboys have emphasized making roster moves that would help them stop the run. The Giants had little problem in that area, however, running 37 times for 165 yards and controlling the clock with relative ease.
It appears the Cowboys have some quality pieces on defense, most notably Williams and rookie defensive back Caleb Downs, but the overall talent looked thin Sunday night. There were notable weaknesses on all three levels.
“This is a humbling business,” Schottenheimer said. “We got humbled tonight. That’s what I told the guys. We lost Mile 1 of a 17-mile marathon.”
What prevents him from watching that performance and thinking the defense was similar to last season?
“Every day we went against them in practice,” Schottenheimer responded. “The defense we saw in practice was not what we saw tonight.”
One game is too soon to panic. It’s realistic to think a team that doesn’t play its starters in the preseason could make a significant jump in Week 2. But there was too much bad to not be somewhat concerned.
The offense has the weapons to put up points against any team, but the absence of standout left guard Tyler Smith was felt against the Giants, particularly in the run game early.
“I’m still optimistic,” Prescott said. “That doesn’t change our goals. It doesn’t change how we feel about our team. This is a marathon. It’s a long season. We’re going to respond.”
Defensively, the inside linebacker play wasn’t great and starting middle linebacker DeMarvion Overshown left the game early with a hamstring injury. Starting safety Malik Hooker left with what is feared to be a fractured forearm.
Physically, the Giants had the edge. There wasn’t enough pass rush from the Cowboys and there weren’t many opportunities where Dart was forced to throw the ball into a risky space.
Mentally, New York made fewer costly errors. Overshown hit Dart out of bounds early on a key play to get things going for the Giants. Running back Javonte Williams uncharacteristically held the ball out to a defender as he was crossing the goal line late in the game, leading to a taunting penalty that pushed back the point-after attempt from Brandon Aubrey, which he missed.
Combine all of that and the recipe that beat the Cowboys on Sunday night will be copied going forward: keep their talented offense on the sideline as much as possible, establish the run game and put together long drives that eat up the majority of the clock. The Giants had the ball for more than 13 minutes longer than the Cowboys.
Many have been skeptical of those singing the Cowboys’ praises for how quietly things were during the offseason. The vibe had been feeling different around the team for the first time in the last three years. There was a lot of positive momentum.
But maybe this outcome just shows why Jones was feeling so anxious an hour before kickoff Sunday night.
“I know the way we approach things,” Prescott said. “I know that our routine, I know that our standard, I know that the way we practice is the right way. My message is echoing, ‘Don’t change, don’t flinch, don’t blink.’ This is a long year. We have to stick together. We’re hanging our hat on our brotherhood and that’s who we believe that we are, so there’s no better time to show than after a loss.
“A little bit of adversity, we got to make sure that we use it as a lesson.”

full_text:
“He’s super cerebral and such a smart guy, but he’s also a guy’s guy,” Broncos backup quarterback Jarrett Stidham says of new play caller Davis Webb. Kevin C. Cox / Getty Images
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Kliff Kingsbury sent Eric Morris on a fact-finding mission shortly after being hired as the head coach at Texas Tech in December of 2012.
Morris, brought on as offensive coordinator, sped down a series of lonely Texas highways to watch a teenager named Davis Webb throw the ball. Webb, a nationally ranked recruit from Prosper High School, had six months earlier committed to Texas Tech and previous head coach Tommy Tuberville. Kingsbury liked Webb’s tape and his pedigree as a coach’s son, but he wanted Morris to get an up-close look at the passer and report back before they decided to move forward with Webb as their quarterback.
“It might have been my first assignment,” Morris said. “Kliff just wanted to check off watching him throw and make sure we liked everything about him. So I’m watching him throw into the net. He’s 6-5, 200-plus pounds and he can make any throw on the field, ripping it everywhere. His personality: You could tell he just ate up football at a young age. I called back Kliff and said it was definitely a yes.”
A month later, Webb arrived in Lubbock to get a head start on his true freshman season. It didn’t take long for Morris, Kingsbury, and just about everyone else to realize their newest recruit was destined for a football career that would extend well beyond his days as a quarterback.
“Davis was someone who we all said, even from a young age, was going to be a phenomenal coach,” said Morris, now the head coach at Oklahoma State. “It was something you could see. He wanted as much information as you could give him. He was constantly in our offices. ‘What if we did this? What if we did that?’ … His rise in coaching hasn’t shocked any of us who were around him.”
Webb, 13 years after that freshman year as a quarterback at Texas Tech, will call his first regular-season NFL game Monday night as the Broncos’ offensive coordinator. Sean Payton, for the first time in his two decades as an NFL head coach, decided to hand off play calling to someone else. He chose an assistant half his age — literally, Payton is 62; Webb is 31 — because he believes Webb “has a gift” that will help elevate Denver’s offense during a season that arrives with championship expectations. In his first game in the role, Webb will square off against the Kansas City Chiefs and veteran defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo, who was the interim head coach of the New York Giants in 2017, when Webb was a rookie quarterback working behind Eli Manning.
“I was the scout-team quarterback, and back in the day, only the defensive players and myself got banana pudding from his wife,” Webb said of playing for Spagnuolo. “ … He’s one of the greatest defensive coordinators in this game’s history. It will be a tough challenge for us out of the gate.”
It can all seem like a meteoric rise for Webb. Reminders of how recently he played the game are everywhere. When he dialed up a play in the preseason that got Jaylen Waddle open for a big gain, Webb joked that the play was all the sweeter because it happened in front of Packers defensive back Xavier McKinney, his former Giants teammate. Another of his teammates in New York was Evan Engram, now the featured tight end in Denver’s passing game. When Webb made the only start of his NFL career, during a second stint with the Giants in 2022, one of the players blocking for him was offensive tackle Matt Peart, now a reserve lineman in Denver.
To view Webb as the NFL’s next new-kid-on-the-block coaching wunderkind, though, would be to discount all that has gone into preparing himself for the moment that arrives Monday night.
“He’s been prepped and has been waiting for this day,” quarterback Bo Nix said, “for a long time.”
Peart describes Webb’s coaching style with two paronymic words: “Intensity and intentionality.”
Both sides of that football personality were encapsulated in Webb’s first meaningful college game. Though he arrived in Lubbock a semester early, Webb was ultimately beat out for the starting job at the beginning of the 2013 season by Baker Mayfield, who had arrived as a walk-on just as fall practices began. In the third game of the season, though, a Thursday night primetime clash with rival TCU, an injury to Mayfield in the fourth quarter of a tie game thrust Webb into action. To that point, Webb had only played — and not particularly well — during mop-up duty in a season-opening blowout of Stephen F. Austin. Still, as he entered the huddle following Mayfield’s injury, the game hanging in the balance, Webb was no shrinking violet.
“He comes in the huddle and says something along the lines of, ‘Alright, boys, daddy’s home. Let’s go win this thing!” said Bradley Marquez, a former Tech wide receiver and Webb’s close friend. “He just commanded it. To be able to come in, in a pressure moment, he just kept everybody relaxed and ready to rock.”
Moments later, Webb hit Marquez for a touchdown pass to give the Red Raiders the lead. Later, after Tech added a field goal to stretch the lead to 10 points, he was alone on the sidelines, practicing the victory-formation kneeldown, no detail too small.
“There was always so much time and effort he put into making sure things were right,” Morris said.
Still, Webb had to learn how to tailor his message. Morris said the quarterback had a wholesale grasp of Kingsbury’s system so quickly that he would, at times, get angry with teammates who weren’t in the right spots because they hadn’t mastered the plan’s concepts. He learned that a one-size-fits-all approach to correcting mistakes wouldn’t work.
“I think that comes off the wrong way at times,” Morris said. “But now, being around him, I’ve seen him mature so much. He knows how to channel that and provide information in a different way where people want to listen to that information.”
Webb honed that skill during his playing career. He would play safety on the scout team in Buffalo to make sure Josh Allen had the right look during game prep. When the Bills traded for Stefon Diggs in March of 2020 at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, Webb met the team’s new star wide receiver on Zoom three times a week to help him grasp the playbook during an offseason that didn’t conclude with OTAs. During Diggs’ first season in Buffalo, he led the NFL with 127 catches and 1,535 yards, both franchise records.
Similarly, Webb helped new players on the Giants install the playbook when he followed Brian Daboll to New York in 2022, taking on the player-coach-type responsibilities that helped him connect with different personalities across the roster. Spagnuolo recalled last week that when Webb was a rookie with the Giants, he would create a tape at the end of each week that was “more or less to test the quarterbacks and what they might see.”
Broncos wide receivers coach Ronald Curry said watching Webb deliver messages to players in meetings now is the perfect balancing act that many young coaches can struggle to nail down.
“He doesn’t mind challenging guys,” said Curry, who is in his first year on Denver’s staff after spending the past two seasons as the quarterbacks coach for the Bills. “The way he runs his meetings, you’ve seen nothing like it. He knows how to get on guys and encourage them in the same sentence, and he keeps it light. He has as bright a future as anyone I’ve been around.”
Broncos backup quarterback Jarrett Stidham has known Webb for roughly 15 years. Stidham was committed to Texas Tech for the 2014 season before ultimately signing with Baylor. Later, they were opposing quarterbacks when the two teams played late in that campaign. Stidham has always admired Webb’s obsession with the success of others, from teammates to fellow coaches. It’s a principle that guides his teaching style.

title: New season, same Packers: Another embarrassing collapse in 39-22 loss to Vikings The Vikings scored 29 unanswered points in the second half in a movie that looked all too familiar to the Packers and their fans. Matt Schneidman 126
summary:
Packers quarterback Jordan Love threw for 387 yards and two touchdowns, but his two fourth-quarter turnovers were too much to overcome. Stephen Maturen / Getty Images
MINNEAPOLIS — The cut-and-paste buttons on this computer might get a lot of work this season.
That’s the best way to describe what happened on Sunday at U.S. Bank Stadium.
This may be a new season for the Green Bay Packers. But right now, after a 39-22 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , this looks like the same old team.
Packers 13, B
full_text:
Packers quarterback Jordan Love threw for 387 yards and two touchdowns, but his two fourth-quarter turnovers were too much to overcome. Stephen Maturen / Getty Images
MINNEAPOLIS — The cut-and-paste buttons on this computer might get a lot of work this season.
That’s the best way to describe what happened on Sunday at U.S. Bank Stadium.
This may be a new season for the Green Bay Packers. But right now, after a 39-22 loss to the Minnesota Vikings , this looks like the same old team.
Packers 13, Bears 3, 33 seconds left in the third quarter
Packers 21, Bears 3, halftime
Packers 22, Vikings 10, 5:09 left in the third quarter
Not counting a meaningless Week 18 game last season in which the Packers rested their starters against the Vikings, those are Green Bay’s last three games against NFC North opponents. They had double-digit, second-half leads in all three. Week 16 last season with the division on the line; the wild-card round with their season at stake; Week 1 in 2026 with a golden opportunity to start anew.
The Packers lost each of those games.
All offseason, they emphasized finishing better, but that appears to have been all talk. The Packers still can’t walk the walk. Instead, they stumbled, tripped and fell flat on their faces yet again.
“It’s going to be a topic of conversation for all you guys until we do it,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “That’s the bottom line.”
Collapses come in different shapes and sizes. They can be defined by a muffed Romeo Doubs onside-kick recovery, blown coverages on the back end against Caleb Williams or an offensive line that looks more like a set of subway turnstiles than five 300-plus-pound behemoths paid to keep a $220 million quarterback on his feet.
Does LaFleur deserve blame? Of course. He’s not on the field, but he’s in charge of setting the culture and identity for one of the most iconic franchises in sports. The Packers’ identity is that of a team that can’t shut the door, one that crumbles when momentum turns in a hostile away environment. This would be a Week 1 overreaction, but we saw it all last season, too, and a lot of the same core players remain with the head coach.
Have there been exceptions to this identity? Yes, like on Thanksgiving in Detroit last season, when the Packers did the opposite. But in their last six road non-wins (while playing their starters), the Packers led by at least nine points in each: at Cleveland (loss) and Dallas (tie) early last season, at Denver (loss), twice at Chicago (losses) and then at Minnesota on Sunday.
Phrases like “we have to finish better” and “we are the only ones who can beat us” and “we have to go do it now instead of just talking about it” carry little meaning now. They are simply hollow words yet to be backed by meaningful action.
We all attended a movie Sunday in Minnesota that we’ve seen before. If you were surprised by the ending, that’s on you.
“Gotta be able to go out there and … look across the line of scrimmage and say, ‘That guy is not going to beat me,’” tight end Tucker Kraft said. “It pisses me off just as much as it does the coaches when we’re out there, and we’re just error after error — like we’re just beating ourselves. I emphasize that all the time. The only people who can beat us are us. That’s it. We’re the best team in the NFL, but if we don’t go out there and play like it, no one’s going to believe us.”
As things stand, nobody believes that. And nobody should.
Much like a handful of Packers losses last season, this one began with a tease. One of the team’s least-appreciated players by fans, cornerback Keisean Nixon, had a tackle for loss and interception on the first two defensive plays of the season. Rookie kicker Trey Smack made a 59-yard field goal on his first regular-season attempt. Wide receiver Christian Watson caught all five targets for 131 yards and two touchdowns in the first half. No Micah Parsons, no problem, as the defense was flying around and making plays. Quarterback Jordan Love, despite constant pressure in his face, showed why he’s one of the NFL’s best.
But the Packers let Carson Wentz and the Vikings hang around by settling for too many field goals or no points at all. As more time passed and Minnesota remained within striking distance, nightmares of last season morphed into reality.
“You look at that fourth quarter, they got the momentum, and they started rolling, and that’s where we kind of fell apart,” Love said. “I think obviously being in this away environment, the noise … the communication has got to be 100 percent. That’s where the momentum gets going, and we’ve got to be able to be at our best still and overcome that stuff. And I don’t think we did.”
The momentum shifted after Smack made a 40-yard field goal to put the Packers up eight with 13:17 remaining. The Vikings were flagged for offside on the fourth-and-6 kick attempt, so LaFleur accepted the penalty and kept his offense on the field for fourth-and-1. Love’s QB sneak was stuffed to keep the lead at 22-17. Love said he could’ve waited for the rush before diving forward instead of going up the middle right away.
“We’re going to be aggressive,” LaFleur said. “It was going to be an eight-point game. If it would have been a two-possession game, I probably would have thought otherwise. … Sometimes you live and die by that, but we’re going to be aggressive, and we’re going to try to go for the throat in that situation.
“They gave us a look for the quarterback sneak. We checked to it, and we didn’t get it.”
On the ensuing Vikings drive, the Packers made three third-down stops, but each one was negated by a defensive penalty (the Packers committed 12 penalties in the game for 98 yards). Illegal contact by defensive back Javon Bullard took away a third-and-11 sack that would’ve forced a punt. Roughing the passer by rookie defensive tackle Chris McClellan killed a third-and-3 incompletion that might’ve forced another punt. And defensive holding by safety Xavier McKinney cost Green Bay a third-and-5 interception in the end zone by safety Evan Williams.
The very next play, future Packers Hall of Famer Aaron Jones ran in for the go-ahead score. Justin Jefferson caught the two-point conversion for a three-point lead, and the Vikings never looked back. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores turned up the heat on Love, who turned the ball over twice in the final five minutes. He stood no chance in the pocket. This might be a topic for another day, but the offensive line is a problem. We knew it might be entering the season, and that skepticism came to fruition.
The Packers have known Flores and his chaotic pressure schemes were first on the schedule for months. But it looked at times like Green Bay’s players and coaches found out last night. According to Next Gen Stats, Vikings linebacker Blake Cashman generated seven quick pressures, the most by an off-ball linebacker in a game since at least 2018. NGS also noted that the Vikings’ 78.3-percent blitz rate was the fourth-highest in a game by any defense since at least 2018. Love threw for 189 yards and two touchdowns in the first half when blitzed, but the Vikings had four sacks and an interception on second-half blitzes. The Vikings tallied a whopping 15 quarterback hits, led by edge rusher Dallas Turner’s seven.
“You never know where it’s coming from, when it’s coming, because they make it all look the same,” right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele said. “That’s kinda like their whole M.O.”
The good news for the Packers? It’s only Week 1. They have plenty of talent and plenty of season left.
The bad news? Why should we believe anything will be different? That they’ll consistently hold onto big leads if and when they get them? Parsons’ return might help rectify that problem since he’s the ultimate closer — former Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley likened him to Mariano Rivera last season — but are Green Bay’s problems too deep for a single player to fix?
Perhaps there should be more urgency, even if it’s just one game.…

Houston’s C.J. Stroud and Carolina’s Bryce Young combined for five touchdown passes while quarterbacking Week 1 offenses that topped 30 points. Both lost against 2025 playoff teams led by quarterbacks with Tier 1 credentials (Josh Allen, who led Buffalo at Houston, 36-31) or Tier 1 potential (Caleb Williams, who led Chicago to a 59-37 victory at Carolina).
The obvious differences between Allen/Williams and Stroud/Young should make any team pause before entering into a top-of-market deal with a mid-tier quarterback.
Stroud’s production to this point in his career includes a No. 20 ranking in EPA per pass play, about the same as the rankings for Trevor Lawrence (21st) and Kyler Murray (22nd) when those players signed top-of-market extensions with Jacksonville and Arizona, respectively.
Young’s No. 34 ranking in EPA per pass play since entering the league tracks with the No. 33 ranking for Daniel Jones when Jones re-signed with the Giants. Young has been trending positively, but he still ranks only 25th among 32 qualifying quarterbacks since the start of last season (Stroud ranks 14th on that list).
The chart above stacks 10 quarterbacks drafted in the first round from 2018-23 by how quickly they received second contracts. Lawrence, Murray, Allen and Joe Burrow signed new deals after three seasons, the earliest allowed under labor rules. Jones and Tagovailoa waited as questions about their abilities lingered. Lamar Jackson's situation was a one-off in that he was a former MVP operating without an agent, which complicated negotiations.
The bottom line: Teams with significant questions about their quarterbacks through three seasons — the Giants with Jones, the Dolphins with Tagovailoa — regretted those decisions enough for others to preserve their flexibility.

Nothing compares to experiencing the first round of March Madness in a Las Vegas sportsbook, but I would add the first NFL Sunday to any fan’s bucket list.

full_text:
Justin Herbert and the Los Angeles Chargers lost to the Arizona Cardinals as the biggest betting favorites of Week 1. Keith Birmingham / MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images
Nothing compares to experiencing the first round of March Madness in a Las Vegas sportsbook, but I would add the first NFL Sunday to any fan’s bucket list.
With the growth of fantasy football and proliferation of player prop betting, the energy has intensified on every single play. My biggest takeaway from engulfing myself in a Vegas book for the umpteenth time was the cheering and screaming every time a player approached the end zone. Simply put, every play now seemingly has higher stakes and thus more engagement.
Let’s recap this first Sunday, then glean some actionable information for Week 2 and beyond.
Sunday’s biggest domino was undoubtedly the Los Angeles Chargers laying a giant egg and losing as 9.5-point home favorites to the Arizona Cardinals — the largest Week 1 upset since 2018.
This nuked numerous moneyline parlays and survivor pool entries, with the Chargers being the most popular pick on Yahoo (more than 32 percent). Most notably, the infamous Circa Survivor saw nearly one-third of its record 25,017 entries (at $1,000 each) bounced by the Bolts — and by the way, include me in the carnage. The eventual winner(s) of $25.017 million will look fondly on avoiding that early landmine.
That’s a tough pill to swallow, considering the Jacksonville Jaguars (-8.5) were an easy pick as similar home favorites over the lowly Cleveland Browns, cruising to a 34-10 win. Cleveland looks like it could be the league’s worst team yet again.
A decade ago, the Browns went 1-31 over a two-year stretch, including 7-24-1 against the spread (ATS), and all it took was one quarter of watching Deshaun Watson’s ineptitude for me to realize we could be in familiar territory.
Looks like another season of oddsmakers struggling to make these Browns spreads high enough
— Doug Kezirian (@DougKezirian) September 13, 2026
While the Chargers crushed bettors in the late slate, the peak drama came during the early slate in Detroit, with parlays and survivor entries experiencing the full range of emotion — from rocking-chair winner to sweating overtime.
The New Orleans Saints trailed the Detroit Lions, 21-0, midway through the third quarter with a live moneyline of +7800 at DraftKings — but those long-shot tickets fell just short of cashing (a $10 bet would have paid out $780). Tyler Shough’s two-point pass attempt sailed over Noah Fant, allowing Detroit to avoid the near-collapse with a 31-30 victory in overtime.
Recreational bettors love to risk a little to win a lot. That is a prevailing concept since casinos invented slots and sportsbooks created parlays. However, that dopamine rush has spiked even higher in recent years with parlays involving proposition bets. For the NFL, that means touchdowns and same-game parlays.
A small roar occurred early in the day when Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor scored his game’s first touchdown against the Baltimore Ravens, cashing a -190 parlay piece for many public bettors who figured he would deliver yet again after leading the league with 20 total touchdowns last season.
A much larger roar broke out when Carolina Panthers tight end Darren Waller caught a ball in the end zone against the Chicago Bears, seemingly cashing a +2500 ticket for the game’s first TD. That was quickly met with a sigh once a referee announced offensive pass interference.
“Our props grow every year,” DraftKings Sportsbook director Johnny Avello told The Athletic . “Going back to the retail environment, the biggest time was the Super Bowl and maybe the playoffs. We put up some during the week but it wasn’t a large variety. Now we are doing it for every game and expanding on them, including first touchdown and anytime TD and then multiple TDs.”
I sat with friends who wagered on Jahmyr Gibbs of the Detroit Lions recording at least 15 yards rushing in every quarter with +425 odds at Caesars Sportsbook. Approaching halftime, Detroit’s defense forced a New Orleans punt in the final half-minute. Two plays later, from the Lions’ own 9-yard line, Gibbs took the shotgun handoff and ran for a seemingly “meaningless” 11 yards — that pushed his rushing total over the 15-yard mark for the quarter and ultimately cashed my friends’ +425 tickets.
We no longer have to wait for the Super Bowl for seemingly every play to impact prop bets.
You know what helps cashing those types of prop bets? High-scoring games.
With Monday Night Football still to go, this is on pace to be the highest-scoring Week 1 since the 1969-70 merger. That’s particularly surprising, given the midweek games each cruised under their totals.
Then again, a game involving nearly 100 points will skew those numbers. The Chicago Bears played like the team head coach Ben Johnson told The Athletic he wanted them to be this season: “the highest-scoring offense ever.” They finished Sunday as the highest-scoring team of the week with a 59-37 win at the Carolina Panthers. That, coupled with the surprising shootout in Houston that saw the Buffalo Bills beat the Texans 36-31, made history.
With Bears/Panthers, we have two games over total in Week 1 at the half for first time in 30+ yrs https://t.co/tTdRWSZDvX
— Evan Abrams (@EvanHAbrams) September 13, 2026
Nine of Sunday’s 13 games have cashed the over, which is a surprising result. Entering the day, Week 1 unders were 54-22 over the last four seasons and 25-9 over the last two-plus seasons.
One thing worth filing away for this Thursday night and the rest of the season: Over the last two-plus seasons, no NFL quarterback has a better betting record in the second half than Josh Allen. After Sunday’s game-winning touchdown drive, the former MVP is now 30-9 ATS, which matches his ranking in advanced stats after halftime.
The guy adjusts and delivers.

full_text:
Justin Herbert, Jim Harbaugh and Mike McDaniel celebrated just two touchdowns in Sunday's 26-14 loss. Harry How / Getty Images
INGLEWOOD, Calif. — Jim Harbaugh spoke slowly. Haltingly. Almost dazed as he tried to wrap his mind around the Los Angeles Chargers’ season-opening 26-14 loss to the Arizona Cardinals.
In an NFL Week 1 contest at SoFi Stadium, the Chargers should have unveiled their newly redesigned offense in grand fashion, lighting up the scoreboard against an opponent who, on paper, appeared dramatically inferior.
Instead, the unit directed by heralded new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel largely stumbled and fumbled its way through the afternoon and, much to the Chargers’ surprise, never managed to produce any kind of sustained success.
“There were quite a few things,” Harbaugh said. “Much to get better at. … It’s not the start that we wanted, but credit to the Cardinals. And it’ll be about our resolve, our way we bounce back.”
The Chargers had enjoyed loads of feel-good vibes about McDaniel leading up to Sunday. Harbaugh hired McDaniel, the former Miami Dolphins head coach regarded as one of the NFL’s brightest offensive minds, in January with the goal of elevating quarterback Justin Herbert and the offense to an elite level. Harbaugh and McDaniel described their partnership as a perfect match. McDaniel repeatedly praised Herbert for his impressive skill set and potential within the system and how those gifts would enable him to expand his playbook like never before.
Last season, the Chargers ranked 12th in offensive yards (333.8 per game) but 19th in points (21.6). They were among the worst at converting in the red zone (45.76 percent). McDaniel was supposed to quickly correct the problem areas.
So after weeks and months of encouraging practices, the Chargers’ players and coaches were stunned by Sunday’s mistakes. They scored just once in each half, and they turned the ball over on downs three times and crossed midfield only once in the second half.
The Chargers were flat-out bad.
“Definitely a little surprised,” left tackle Rashawn Slater said. “I think it was uncharacteristic of us.”
“It’s the feeling of you get punched,” Harbaugh said. “And how we respond is what I’m thinking about right now.”
The Chargers on Sunday received a valuable lesson that it’s not enough to have a fancy new playbook bursting with endless possibilities and exquisitely designed plays. Even the most creative play caller can’t overcome sloppy, undisciplined play and inattention to detail.
Herbert played just seven snaps in two preseason cameos, so the Chargers didn’t have a true indication of whether their new offensive architect had shored up the weak areas. But briefly Sunday, it appeared as if the Chargers would dazzle despite the lack of an expansive dress rehearsal.
The offense cruised downfield on its first possession, scoring a touchdown (an Omarion Hampton 8-yard run) to cap an eight-play, 77-yard drive in which Herbert completed all three of his pass attempts to wide receiver Ladd McConkey for 60 yards. And Los Angeles displayed promise on its second series until Hampton fumbled at the Arizona 30-yard line roughly 90 seconds into the second quarter.
Later that quarter, the Chargers marched 66 yards on 10 plays, reaching the Arizona 3 before stalling and facing fourth-and-goal. Down 10-7, Harbaugh could have opted for a chip-shot field goal to tie the score with 1:55 left in the half. Instead, he went for it, only to see a fierce pass rush up the gut led by Cardinals defensive tackle Dante Stills overwhelm Herbert for a sack, a loss of 10 yards and a turnover on downs.
From there, the Chargers never fully recovered. They punted to open the second half. They did score on a three-play, 60-yard drive (largely made possible by a 48-yard pass interference penalty on Arizona) capped by a Herbert-to-McConkey toss. But the Chargers never crossed midfield again, their possessions ending with a punt, a blocked punt, an interception and two turnovers on downs.
Adding insult to injury, McConkey left the game with a chest injury midway through the fourth quarter and did not return. He led the Chargers with five catches for 82 yards and the touchdown.
Five penalties, misalignments, errant passes, blown blocking assignments, a sputtering rushing attack and a turnover combined to cripple the offense. Meanwhile, the Cardinals turned a one-score halftime lead into a double-digit advantage by game’s end.
Disappointment hung heavy in a relatively silent locker room after the game. Numerous players departed before reporters entered.
“We just have to execute … to not have penalties,” Herbert (17-for-27 for 209 yards, a touchdown, an interception and three sacks) said during a postgame news conference. “We’ve got to score in the red zone. We didn’t execute those third downs, and we didn’t move the ball that we needed to. They played well, but it’s on us to play better. It’s on us to go score points, make sure that we’re doing everything we can on third down in the red zone and limiting turnovers.”
Herbert dismissed the notion that the struggles stemmed from a lack of real game time in the offense.
“We’ve run those plays since OTAs and since (training) camp, so we know them, and we just have to go out there and do what we know we’re capable of,” he said. “(Newness) hasn’t been an issue at all. So we’re going to watch the film and see where we went wrong and what we can learn from it.”
Although troubled by the performance, Harbaugh refused to sound any alarms and instead declared confidence in his players.
“We have to tackle them all,” he said, referring to the problem areas. “I know the type of competitors we have, and I know there’ll be a big bounce back.”
Slater echoed his coach’s sentiments.
“You know, it’s Week 1,” the sixth-year veteran said. “Not to make an excuse, but at the same time, I don’t think we’re going to be looking at Week 1 come Week 16. So, we just have to keep rolling, keep getting better, and that’s what it’s all about.”
