full_text:
Jim Harbaugh (left), Justin Herbert (No. 10) and Mike McDaniel left plenty to second-guess in Sunday's loss to the Cardinals. Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images
Two NFL head coaches made bold proclamations heading into the 2026 season.
One of them looks smarter than the other today.
Ben Johnson said his Chicago Bears hoped to average 38 points per game , enough to set a single-season scoring record. Jim Harbaugh said his Los Angeles Chargers quarterback, Justin Herbert, would go down as the greatest in league history .
After Johnson’s Bears ran all over Carolina’s defense during a 59-37 victory, Harbaugh’s Chargers fell 26-14 at home to the Arizona Cardinals , who entered Week 1 as the heaviest underdog (+10.5) by far.
The first Pick Six column of this new season leads with an analysis of the Chargers’ dispiriting opener and a look at why Herbert won’t become the best QB in franchise history, let alone the league.
We’ll also run through how all the new offensive play callers fared, from the Chargers’ Mike McDaniel to Baltimore’s Declan Doyle (41 points!) and Cleveland’s Todd Monken (49 plays!). We’ll include Buffalo’s Joe Brady (409 yards against Houston’s defense!) now that he’s calling plays as a head coach for the first time. The full menu:
• About that Herbert GOAT talk • Doyle, Monken and new callers • Rams, Panthers paid for this? • Why Rams should be concerned • Stroud, Young and second deals • Two-minute drill: Cards and Vikes
A defensive coach who has faced Herbert multiple times compares and contrasts the Chargers’ quarterback to Josh Allen.
Both are a tick slower than most top quarterbacks at seeing the game and processing it, this coach said. That gives defenses a chance to counter their superior athletic and throwing ability. The way the defensive coach sees things, Allen has been in the same offense long enough to improve his processing (this is his fourth season with Brady calling plays). That has helped him ascend. Herbert, in contrast, is on his fifth offensive coordinator in seven NFL seasons.
“I still like the guy and think he’s good,” this defensive coach said of Herbert. “But if he does have a little success, Mike (McDaniel) will get a new job as a head coach. He just has to have a decent year, and the cycle will continue for the quarterback.”
Both the Bills and Chargers have invested resources into building strong offensive lines for their quarterbacks. While Buffalo has succeeded, the Chargers have struggled. Injuries at tackle wiped out their line last season. Weakness on the interior figures to be a problem this season, giving Herbert less time to process.
Sunday’s first impression was not encouraging, as the Chargers managed just 14 points and 268 yards against a defense that finished 28th in EPA per play last season. The chest injury that knocked top receiver Ladd McConkey from the game in the third quarter marked a turning point. The Chargers averaged 6.3 yards on the 26 plays with McConkey on the field but only 4.2 across the 25 plays without him. Herbert’s EPA per pass play plummeted from +0.22 to -0.33.
As for Harbaugh, he’ll remain the ultimate cheerleader for his quarterback.
“Justin Herbert, when it’s all said and done, when his career comes to an end, I predict he will be known as the greatest, best ever to play the position of quarterback,” Harbaugh said heading into this season.
The comment recalled what Harbaugh said in 2011 about Alex Smith, then his quarterback with the 49ers.
“He’s every bit the elite quarterback as there is playing in the game right now,” Harbaugh said then.
Smith had tossed 10 touchdowns while going 7-1 as a starter under Harbaugh to that point, ranking 21st in EPA per pass play. Aaron Rodgers had 24 touchdown passes over the same period. Drew Brees had 21. Tom Brady had 20. Smith was not nearly as elite as those guys, but Harbaugh didn’t care.
The interesting thing about Herbert is not whether he’ll go down as the “greatest, best ever” quarterback in league history. That isn’t happening. The interesting part is whether Herbert can make anything close to the jump his long-ago Hall of Fame Chargers predecessor, Dan Fouts, made at the same point in his career.
Fouts, like Herbert, was solid but unspectacular for the Chargers during his first six NFL seasons.
Fouts ranked fifth in yards per attempt and 12th in passer rating among 24 quarterbacks with at least 40 starts over his first six seasons, commanding zero MVP votes. His career trajectory changed when Don Coryell took over as the Chargers' head coach entering his seventh season. Fouts then ranked first in yards per attempt and second to Joe Montana in passer rating over the next six seasons. He was named first-team All-Pro twice and finished among the top six in MVP voting four times.
Herbert will never play for Coryell, who was elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame posthumously in 2023. He is getting to play for the only coach since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger to score 70 points in a game. But McDaniel probably won't be with the Chargers for the long term, and the Chargers' offensive depth is concerning, especially if McConkey misses time.
Harbaugh has been at his best when able to assemble an all-star staff. He sets the tone but isn't a differentiating offensive designer able to elevate an offense by himself. Longer term, Herbert might need the Chargers to hire the next Coryell, not the next Harbaugh.
It was only one week. It must be better next week against the Raiders, ahead of a seven-game stretch against the Bills, Seahawks, Broncos, Chiefs, Rams, Texans and Ravens, with five of those on the road.
"They are going to have their hands full with the Raiders next week," another coach said, "because the Raiders are organized, they have a veteran quarterback and their defensive front is decent."
NFL offenses averaged more than 24 points per game in Week 1, which would be the highest for an opening week this century if it holds through Monday night. Teams were under center on early downs 50.4 percent of the time, the highest rate for any week since the 2017 season. The final week of the 2025 season ranks second at 47.1 percent, affirming a trend that is helping offenses present a run threat more convincingly.
Coaches can be quick to offer theories as to why. The absence of offseason tackling and preseason reps rank high on their list, but those aren't new developments. A quick look at preseason playing time over the past eight seasons showed no correlation.
And so we'll give some of these offenses their due. The jobs Arizona's Mike LaFleur, Las Vegas' Klint Kubiak and the New York Jets' Frank Reich executed Sunday stand apart because those three offensive play callers revived units that ranked 21st (Cardinals), 29th (Jets) and 31st (Raiders) in EPA per play last season. And all three won.
We begin with the offensive play callers burdened not by their teams' recent struggles, but rather those leading offenses where good might not be good enough. Brady, the Bills' offensive play caller since 2023, makes the list because this is his first season calling plays without having to run the game plan past the head coach.
Joe Brady, Bills: Allen's numbers in two games against Houston over the past two seasons were far worse than they were against seven other opponents he faced more than once over that span. His passer rating (62.2), yards per attempt (6.0), completion percentage (51.6) and EPA per pass play (-0.11) in those two losses at Houston were all evidence that the Texans' defense was on the verge of becoming legendary .
This Bills performance ranks No. 1 against the Texans in 39 total games over the past three seasons by points scored (36), EPA per play (0.28), yards per play (8.1) and yards per pass attempt (11.5). It validated the Bills' standing as the No. 1 team in the AFC, as projected by league executives heading into the season. Big relief for Bills fans.

( Editor’s note: This is excerpted from Mike Sando’s Pick Six of Sept. 14, 2026.)
The Rams’ 27-7 defeat to the 49ers in Australia felt like more than just one game.
“This will define us only if we allow it to,” McVay said after the game.
There was gravity to McVay’s words and delivery, followed a bit later in his postgame media session with some contextualizing: “This story is far from written.”
Just one game, right? Maybe.
This was the Rams’ ninth-worst defeat by point margin in McVay’s 166 total games as coach.
“The dream teams, the amount of pressure those teams put on themselves, they have to be perfect in every facet,” a coach with no ties to McVay said. “It looks good on paper, but the human component makes it challenging.”
The Myles Garrett situation bears watching after the Rams' blockbuster offseason acquisition missed time during camp to rest a sore knee, played far below his standards in the opener and then landed on injured reserve so he could have arthroscopic surgery . He will miss at least four weeks.
Delicate situations involving superstar players can test relationships between coaches, executives, doctors, trainers, the player and his representatives. In this case, those relationships are new.
Some who played and worked with Garrett during his nine-year career in Cleveland described him as a supremely competitive game day force who does his own thing to get ready during the week. They saw the potential for tension in the way this game played out, and how Garrett spoke after the game.
"I didn't feel I was the player I've been before when I stepped on the field (in Australia)," Garrett said. "I gotta do what I can to get back to that."
Garrett said he was not questioning the Rams' contrarian decision to arrive in Australia just 28 hours before kickoff , a week after the 49ers arrived. How could anyone not question it?
Sports scientists I spoke with said the Rams were spot-on in their handling of the sleep component, but they risked players feeling heavy-legged because it takes time for fluid buildup in the legs to dissipate following such a long flight. The problem can be exacerbated for bigger players like Garrett, who for the first time in his career played at least 55 snaps without recording even one tackle.
"When Myles said he needed to change and do whatever he needed to get himself ready, I took that as either he did not buy into what the team was doing, or there was another ailment going on," a former Browns assistant said. "It was probably a little bit of both."
It's all reading between the lines at this point.

full_text:
Klint Kubiak is 1-0 as an NFL head coach. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
LAS VEGAS — Klint Kubiak was giddy.
He jumped to high-five fans as he ran off the field, victorious in his first game as an NFL head coach. He felt the love afterward in the locker room, where he was given a game ball by general manager John Spytek and engulfed by gleeful players.
“It meant a lot to me,” Kubiak said of the celebration. “Really appreciative of the guys. It’s great to share this moment with them.”
Of course, Raiders coaches have experienced this feeling before. Just over a year ago, they walked into Gillette Stadium and beat the eventual AFC champion New England Patriots in Week 1, giving Pete Carroll a win in his first game as the team’s head coach. After that game, Carroll said they earned the right to enjoy “that kind of fun and (to) cheer on one another.” That sentiment faded fast as the Raiders went on to win two more games over the rest of the season, clinching the league’s worst record and costing Carroll his job.
The Raiders would like to follow a different trajectory this fall. The players believe they can with Kubiak at the helm — second-year wide receiver Jack Bech said the win “definitely does” feel different from the opening win of last year.
“I think just the amount of work, the amount of detail that we have, it’s something like I’ve never been a part of before,” Bech said after the game. “Being able to do this, being able to build on this, come back in tomorrow and get right back to work, it’s gonna be awesome.”
Whether Kubiak can actually bring success over a full season is yet to be determined. And with the Miami Dolphins predicted to be among the league’s worst teams, who knows how much value can be put into Sunday’s win. But Kubiak’s debut provided some signs that better days could be coming, and that he might be the coach to finally bring competency to the franchise.
Las Vegas dominated the trenches against the Dolphins. Quarterback Kirk Cousins wasn’t sacked once, and the running back duo of Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington Jr. combined for 143 yards rushing on just under 4.8 yards per carry. The offensive line was the demise of the Raiders a year ago, when they allowed the league’s most sacks (64) and never gave Jeanty room to run. The addition of prize free-agent center Tyler Linderbaum made an impact, but Kubiak and his staff also got strong performances out of three holdovers from the 2025 team.
Right guard Jackson Powers-Johnson was pleased with how the group played, saying it was “awesome” to open holes for Jeanty to have his third career 100-yard rushing game, adding that keeping Cousins upright was “a point of pride.” But he also believes they can be better.
“I feel like it’s fun, but there’s so much room for growth,” Powers-Johnson said. “That’s the main point of emphasis: that we can get better. That’s the best part about it.”
The Raiders also overcame the loss of Brock Bowers , who missed the season opener after undergoing a recent surgery on his knee. The Pro Bowl tight end was set up to be the focal point of Kubiak’s scheme. Losing a star like Bowers might have torpedoed Raiders teams of old, but Kubiak found ways to move forward, relying on Jeanty and the run game to pace their attack and myriad receivers to pick up the slack.
There were improvements on defense, too. Throughout the preseason, the Raiders struggled to rush the passer and defend the run against non-developmental competition. Quarterbacks had lots of time to throw, and backs such as the Arizona Cardinals’ Jeremiyah Love and Houston Texans’ Woody Marks gashed the Raiders on the ground. Against Miami, Las Vegas totaled five sacks and 17 pressures, according to TruMedia, and held Dolphins star De’Von Achane to just 36 rushing yards.
The Raiders struggled to force turnovers a season ago, with defensive backs totaling just five interceptions. Rookie safety Treydan Stukes was able to notch the team’s first pick Sunday, setting up the offense for its final score. Safety Jeremy Chinn forced a fumble on the Dolphins’ final drive, allowing the Raiders’ offense to salt away a victory.
“All I see is the blurs of the Silver and Black on defense,” Kubiak said. “I love the way our defense played, how they swarmed, how they turned the ball over, how they responded to sudden change. Very proud of them.”
In the postgame locker room, Kubiak told his team to enjoy the moment. His players did, but with a sense of confidence, possibly the biggest sign of change under Kubiak’s leadership.
“This is a new team, new staff, and we’re building a new culture here,” Jeanty said. “And that’s a culture that’s going to win football games.”
The Raiders’ postgame atmosphere was one of self-assurance rather than exuberance. As players recounted the game, they spoke as if they had fulfilled their responsibilities as they should. The team felt like it was supposed to win; there was no surprise in the result.
When asked about the difference between the two season-opening victories, returning players said they feel that this time around they’re staying present. Star pass rusher Maxx Crosby, who had 1.5 sacks in his return from a season-ending knee injury last year, said the team is doing a much better job of “being where we’re at.”
“Every single day and every moment, every meeting, every practice is important,” Crosby said. “Obviously, we’ve got a lot of work to do to get to next Sunday. But just being where our feet are and just taking one day at a time, I think we’ll be exactly where we need to be.”
Instead of focusing on the win, players were already consumed by the steps required to earn the next one. Tight end Michael Mayer, the team’s leader in targets Sunday, said that mindset has been instilled in them by Kubiak.
“We feel really good about this one, but there’s a lot of stuff we’re excited to also clean up,” Mayer said. “There’s kind of an in-between there that Klint’s very good at and that the whole organization is very good at.”
As Mayer talked about his coach’s strengths, Kubiak surprised him from the side and embraced him, as he did many of the players before leaving Allegiant Stadium. Mayer thinks Kubiak is the one who is going to truly change the Raiders as a franchise.
“He’s a great person and a great football mind,” Mayer said. “You just want to learn so much from him, and you’re kind of attracted to his knowledge. You just want to learn everything. And I’ll tell you what: That guy knows a lot about football. He’s been around football. He grew up in football, and I’ve learned so much from him already.”

full_text:
The Carson Wentz-to-Justin Jefferson connection was responsible for six receptions, 81 yards and two touchdowns in Sunday's comeback win over the Packers. Adam Bettcher / Getty Images
MINNEAPOLIS — U.S. Bank Stadium is an architectural marvel. Natural light pokes through the windows, adding a trademark freshness to an indoor coliseum. The jagged edges of the lower bowl almost spotlight the playing field like center stage.
But perhaps the building’s most stunning trait? The way it harnesses energy.
Especially on afternoons like Sunday, when the Minnesota Vikings turn a clunker of a performance into an unforgettable 39-22 comeback against the Green Bay Packers , the momentum shifts feel communal.
“The demeanor of everyone is infectious,” safety Harrison Smith said.
If you could bottle up this emotion, Smith might have stayed at home on his couch.
Fortunately, you can’t. Replicating this type of juice takes this place and these moments.
It takes a failed Jordan Love quarterback sneak attempt on a critical fourth-down attempt. It takes superstar receiver Justin Jefferson diving for the pylon to extend a two-score lead that seemed preposterous based on what came before it. It takes a gutty four-quarter effort, giving coach Kevin O’Connell and the Vikings a chance to make critical week-over-week adjustments without feeling the weight of expectation.
“There are just some games that will stick with you for a long time,” O’Connell said. “Today will be a special one.”
For this victory to be remembered as such, the Vikings must ensure Sunday’s winning formula is not one they continue to follow.
Defensively, they allowed too many explosive plays. Offensively, they were not as efficient running the football as they wanted to be. On a crucial fourth-quarter drive, they cannot rely on three separate Packers penalties to assist their efforts.
“I’m not going to sugarcoat it,” quarterback Carson Wentz, who replaced injured starter Kyler Murray, said. “We had a couple of flags that kept our drive alive. I threw one to their safety (Evan Williams) right in the chest, and it was a flag. So, praise God.”
Maybe most importantly, the more the Vikings have to rely on Wentz early in this season, the more they risk delaying Murray’s acclimation to the offense.
All of these layers matter if the Vikings want to reach their ceiling this season.
However, at a bare minimum, they proved Sunday they won’t be easy to play for four quarters. As long as Jefferson is healthy, and as long as defensive coordinator Brian Flores can adjust his pressure packages midgame to affect opposing offenses, Minnesota can cause headaches.
“When we can get a lead,” linebacker Blake Cashman said, “I don’t think there’s a scarier defense to go against. Especially with the group we have that understands what we’re trying to accomplish.”
Continuity offers the Vikings a way to assess the opponent’s game plan in real time, then adapt. Specifically, Cashman said, Flores and company identified some of Green Bay’s protection answers versus pressure in the first half. Plucking at those holes helped the Vikings bounce back from allowing 19 points in the first half to just 3 in the second.
It also prevented the conversation from centering on explosive plays allowed. The Packers generated seven plays of 20 yards or more Sunday, the second most in a game against Flores’ Vikings since he took over in 2023. Love threw for 387 yards. Give up explosive plays at a similar rate, and the Vikings aren’t likely to be close enough to ignite the energy that came pouring out in the fourth quarter.
By the end of the game, Cashman burst unblocked through the A-gap. Once, he corralled Love, who was stripped of the ball by Vikings edge rusher Andrew Van Ginkel. Another time, Cashman deflected a Love pass that was intercepted by cornerback James Pierre.
These turnovers sent the Vikings sideline into a frenzy. Flores high-stepped. O’Connell fist-pumped. These turnovers also set up touchdowns, alleviating the pent-up stress of the first half.
After months of focus on a revamped rushing attack, the Packers held Vikings running backs to minimal first-quarter gains. Offensive line leakage left Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason with little room.
“Even though we committed to the run,” O’Connell said, “it was not pretty.”
The Vikings averaged 3.6 yards per carry on designed runs, posting one of the lowest rushing-success rates in a game since the beginning of last season.
“They were blitzing from all edges,” right tackle Brian O’Neill said. “It slows you down a little bit, affects running off the ball and combo blocks. We were still worried about if they’re going to move (before and after the snap) because they did move so much on first and second down.”
The ineffective ground game forced the Vikings into suboptimal dropback passing situations.
That’s how, on a third-and-7 in the first quarter, Murray found himself scrambling outside the pocket.
As he scooted toward the first-down marker, Packers defenders Javon Bullard and Lukas Van Ness collided with him as he slid to the ground. His helmet popped off. The Vikings quickly ruled him out with a concussion .
Wentz initially struggled in Murray’s stead, but the seal broke with two minutes remaining until halftime. O’Connell thought the Vikings could catch the Packers unprepared with a cadence adjustment, and he was correct. The adjustment made Van Ness leap across the line of scrimmage before the snap.
Wentz called for the ball, then with the benefit of a free play, he hurled a deep pass to Jefferson down the left sideline. No. 18 toe-tapped the catch in the end zone. It was his first home touchdown since Week 15 of 2024.
“He’s unbelievable,” Wentz said. “The guy is so good. He’s the best in the world at what he does, and sometimes you’ve just got to give him a chance.”
Even after Wentz connected with tight end T.J. Hockenson for a 16-yard touchdown in the third quarter, the Packers still led by a score. Their choice to rescind a successful field goal and try a Love sneak backfired. On the Vikings’ next drive, three separate Packers penalties — all committed on third downs — gave Minnesota’s offense life.
The Vikings spotted an opening and barged through. They cranked up the defensive pressure and made it harder for Love to find open receivers downfield. The O-line sprang Mason for a 28-yard run.
They did the things consistent, good teams do, stirring a hungry crowd that had been waiting for months to pop.

full_text:
Drake Maye went 23-for-33 passing for 178 yards and a touchdown last week against the Seahawks, but his three fourth-quarter interceptions proved too much to overcome. Joe Nicholson / Imagn Images
At the end of the New England Patriots’ season opener Wednesday, they called a play that had long been installed in their playbook, one meant for situations just like this. It was late in the fourth quarter. They were down three points and had third-and-5 at the Seattle Seahawks’ 16-yard line.
Get the ball out quickly. If it’s not there and you have to throw it out of bounds, no worries. Kick a field goal and head to overtime.
But instead of quickly and decisively throwing it to tight end Hunter Henry on an out route, quarterback Drake Maye heaved a pass off his back foot into the end zone toward Mack Hollins, a receiver who is not normally targeted in that passing concept. The ensuing interception, the third of the quarter for Maye, sealed the Patriots’ 13-10 loss .
Of course, that play has been reviewed over and over again. Maye, who was 23-for-33 passing on the day for 178 yards and a touchdown, called it “just unacceptable.”
In the bigger picture, the concern is whether Maye’s four-game playoff slump from last season is carrying over into 2026. As he did in the postseason, Maye made poor decisions and a number of throws he wouldn’t make during his often dominant regular season.
Over those 17 regular-season games a year ago, Maye ranked first among quarterbacks in EPA/play (.313), second in success rate (55 percent), first in yards per attempt (8.9), and first in completion percentage (72). He threw 31 touchdowns and only eight interceptions.
But in Maye’s last five games — four in the playoffs last season and last week’s opener against the Seahawks — he is averaging 6.5 yards per attempt, has completed 60 percent of his passes and has thrown seven touchdowns and seven interceptions.
The hope for New England is that this is just a five-game blip against five talented defenses, including two losses against the Seahawks, arguably the NFL’s top unit.
But there’s a counterpoint to be made. If Maye is truly one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL, as last year’s MVP runner-up performance would suggest, he should be able to perform against the best defenses. Or at least he should’ve looked a lot better after a full offseason to prep for a rematch with the Seahawks, especially entering the game with better receivers and a better offensive line.
Regression from Maye this season was always a possibility. Almost no quarterback other than Patrick Mahomes has been one of the game’s best in both their age-23 and 24 seasons.
But there’s a difference between natural regression after a fairytale season and the dud we saw in Seattle.
Some of it can be chalked up to rust. As part of a growing trend around the league, Maye didn’t play during the preseason. Wednesday night’s action was his first live snaps in a game since the Super Bowl.
“Playing (against) the backups for the Eagles or the Colts for eight plays (in the preseason) was (not) going to prepare us for what we saw (against the Seahawks),” coach Mike Vrabel said last week.
Of course, the problem wasn’t the way Maye started. The issue was that Maye got worse as the game went along.
With the Patriots’ run game struggling and often putting the offense in second- and third-and-long, the Seahawks were content to sit back in deep zones and take away the big plays that Maye was so good at creating a year ago. They wanted to force him into short and underneath passes. In the first three quarters, Maye took what was there for him.
But his patience seemed to wane as the game went along. That’s when we began to see some poor decision-making.
The positive spin would be something like this: Maye rarely played like that a year ago, a much bigger sample size than Wednesday’s opener. He got impatient in his first game in seven months, eager to try and lift his team to a win against an opponent that had just beaten them in the Super Bowl. That level of pressure — and the resulting impatience — are unlikely to remain so high.
It also happened against the league’s best defense from a year ago, a team with a game-planning whiz in coach Mike Macdonald, someone who makes life difficult for pretty much every quarterback.
“We’ve seen Drake perform at an extremely high level, and we anticipate him continuing to do that as we go forward,” Vrabel said. “Drake will learn from it, and hopefully we’ll be better for it in the end.”
This will be an interesting test, though. We’ve never really seen Maye lose a game because of his poor play. As a rookie, the Pats lost plenty, but that was with a terrible roster around him. Last season, even if Maye had some postseason clunkers, he was still doing enough to win games. Or more to the point, he wasn’t directly hurting his team.
How does he bounce back from that?
The Pittsburgh Steelers are up next on Sunday, and even if their defense is pretty good, it’s a far cry from the Seahawks’ unit. Still, the Pats’ home opener will be more important because of the way Wednesday’s game went.
New England can’t afford to open the season 0-2 with back-to-back road games against playoff teams (the Jacksonville Jaguars and Buffalo Bills) up next. And Maye can’t afford another game like that, or else that postseason slump won’t feel so isolated.

full_text:
Jaxson Dart completed a tidy 23 of 29 passes for 230 yards and three TDs in the Giants' opening night win. Elsa / Getty Images
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — New York Giants coach John Harbaugh didn’t put training wheels on his new quarterback. Harbaugh saw the success Jaxson Dart had running an extension of the Ole Miss offense last season as a rookie. But he believed his quarterback needed to be able to handle the complexities of a more conventional NFL offense.
So Harbaugh and his offensive staff, led by offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, put Dart through quarterback school this offseason. There were predictable growing pains as Dart transitioned away from operating an RPO-heavy offense out of the shotgun. But over time, Dart made progress lining up under center and engineering a passing attack that heavily features play-action.
Then on Sunday night, Dart aced his first test. The second-year quarterback had a flawless encore to a promising rookie season. Dart completed 23-of-29 passes for 230 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions in the Giants’ 28-20 statement win over the Cowboys.
“For him to have all this on his plate and to execute the way he did, to me, was just tremendous and very impressive,” Harbaugh said. “It was a great performance by Jaxson.”
No one in the NFL could deny the high-end moments from Dart’s rookie season. His displayed rare playmaking ability when things broke down. The question skeptics had was if Dart could improve at the routine aspects of playing quarterback. Could he resist the urge to hit the eject button from the pocket at the first sign of trouble and instead find simple solutions?
A fourth-quarter drive Sunday night provided strong evidence that Dart has made significant progress in that area. There was nothing flashy about the 13-play, 65-yard touchdown drive that gave the Giants a 28-14 lead to seal the win. Dart was ruthlessly efficient, repeatedly hitting running back Devin Singletary in the left flat as pressure came off the left edge — 12 yards, 7 yards, 9 yards. The third straight completion went for a touchdown.
It was beautifully boring. It’s the type of quarterbacking that will keep Dart far from the blue medical tent on the sideline and keep the Giants’ offense rolling.
“I felt very comfortable. I thought that we just did a really good job of staying in progress throughout the game,” Dart said. “I thought (Nagy) called an awesome game, and I thought the guys just played really, really hard. So it made my job a lot easier, and guys all over the place made a ton of plays, so I’m excited about that.”
For all of the attention paid to Dart’s reckless running style as a rookie, he managed to find the balance on Sunday. His legs were still a weapon, as he had eight carries for 59 yards before three kneeldowns to end the game. He avoided any unnecessary hits by sliding or getting out of bounds. The biggest hit he took was the result of a personal foul by Cowboys linebacker DeMarvion Overshown for leveling him out of bounds at the end of a 22-yard zone-read keeper on the Giants’ opening drive.
The hit took place on the Giants’ sideline, so Overshown was promptly confronted by an army of blue jerseys defending their quarterback.
“The entire team feeds off (Dart’s) energy,” right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said. “You saw what happened when he got hit on the sideline. It was a bulls–t hit. That’s why everyone ran up and defended him. He’s the heartbeat of this team. He’s a leader. We’ll go as far as he takes us.”
The Giants’ protection of Dart extended beyond the sideline skirmish. Dart was only sacked twice, and neither was the fault of the offensive line. One came on a busted play when Dart wisely didn’t throw a screen into danger and slid back to the line of scrimmage. The other came when safety Caleb Downs drilled an unsuspecting Dart off the right edge. Dart fumbled but was fortunate it popped into the arms of left guard Jon Runyan. It didn’t appear that anyone was assigned to block Downs, so it was on Dart to recognize the free blitzer and get the ball out quicker.
The reliable protection allowed Dart to settle into a groove. He completed 10 straight passes during a stretch that spanned from the second quarter to the fourth quarter. The Giants were 9-for-10 on third down before a kneeldown on the final snap of the game.
Dart found his rhythm at the end of the first half when the Giants got the ball back at their 45-yard line after safety Jevon Holland intercepted an egregiously bad pass from Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott. With 49 seconds left in the half and the score tied at 7-7, it was a crucial moment. Things got off to a bad start, with the Giants facing third-and-9 after a Runyan false start.
But Dart then shredded a revamped Cowboys defense that still has a long way to go. First came a 16-yard deep out to wide receiver Malik Nabers in a soft spot in Dallas’ zone coverage. Nabers, who wasn’t sure he’d play until a workout less than two hours before kickoff, finished with six catches for 69 yards while operating on a pitch count that limited him to roughly half the snaps. What Nabers will provide when he’s fully confident in his surgically-repaired knee is a tantalizing thought about the offense’s ceiling.
The Nabers completion was followed by an 18-yard pass to wide receiver Darnell Mooney on a deep out. Then there was a 5-yard out to Isaiah Likely before a 15-yard touchdown strike to the tight end on a corner route against a blown coverage. Likely finished with eight catches for 78 yards and two touchdowns, affirming that his training camp production wasn’t a fluke.
“The O-line did a great job of just showing that we can pass-pro in those situations, in crucial ‘got-to-have-it’ third downs,” Dart said. “And then guys got open, great pass pro, and then made a play, and we were able to capitalize.”
Dart’s biggest development may have come before the snap. Harbaugh, Nagy and Dart have all talked about how much more is on the quarterback’s plate pre-snap in this offense. That was obvious with how many times Dart could be seen adjusting the play at the line of scrimmage.
One instance came in the second quarter when Dart faked a toss to the right and kept the ball around a wide-open left end for a 16-yard gain before wisely scooting out of bounds. He also drew the Cowboys offside with a hard count for a free first down on third-and-1 on the first play of the second quarter.
“I wanted to take it upon myself to do as much as I can,” Dart said. “Even though it was maybe tough, but I felt like it was the best thing for our team to be successful. So I love that part of the game and I think that that’s just going to continue to make me a better player.”
Dart hasn’t sacrificed any of his moxie while becoming a more cerebral quarterback. Asked his mindset after the Cowboys scored to cut the Giants’ lead to 21-14 late in the third quarter, Dart replied flatly, “Let’s go score again.” The Giants did just that, culminating in the 9-yard touchdown pass to Singletary that put the game away.
“He’s a killer,” Eluemunor said. “He really wants to win. He’s locked in on everything. There’s a lot on his plate, but that’s how he likes it.”

title: John Harbaugh's best call of the week? Using his father to motivate the Giants Ian O'Connor 52
summary:

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — John Harbaugh asked his father to speak to the New York Giants on the night before his grand debut, so there stood 87-year-old Jack Harbaugh, facing dozens of young men
full_text:
John Harbaugh, right, celebrates the Giants' win against the Cowboys with his parents, Jack and Jackie. Jack Harbaugh spoke to the team on Saturday night about Muhammad Ali and respect, telling players: "You can’t ask for it, you can’t pray for it. ... You’ve got to demand it." Ian O'Connor / The Athletic
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — John Harbaugh asked his father to speak to the New York Giants on the night before his grand debut, so there stood 87-year-old Jack Harbaugh, facing dozens of young men who, perhaps, could use a little wisdom from a football lifer who has seen it all.
Jack Harbaugh peered into their eyes and was a bit surprised by what was looking back at him. This was, after all, a Giants team that was 25 games under .500 over the past three seasons, matched against an opponent, the Dallas Cowboys, expected to be in Super Bowl contention.
A Cowboys team that has historically owned the Giants as much as John Mara has owned them.
“But these guys were not intimidated,” Jack Harbaugh told The Athletic Sunday night in the winners’ locker room, where he wore a Giants pullover and an FDNY cap.
“People told them, ‘You ought to be this, you weren’t that, you haven’t done this and you haven’t done that.’ But I didn’t see that in their eyes.”
In a team meeting on the eve of their stirring 28-20 victory over the Cowboys , the Giants gave Jack Harbaugh their full attention and respect. The former college and high school coach who won the 2002 Division I-AA national championship at Western Kentucky decided to tell them a story about the man from Louisville he called “the most competitive athlete that I knew in my lifetime. Muhammad Ali.”
Jack Harbaugh explained that during a 1967 fight in the Houston Astrodome, Ali battered heavyweight champ Ernie Terrell, who had repeatedly referred to Ali by his birth name, Cassius Clay. “What’s my name?” Ali had shouted at Terrell in the ring.
“So I talked to the players about respect,” Jack Harbaugh said. “You can’t ask for it, you can’t pray for it, and you can’t expect it. You’ve got to reach out and you’ve got to demand it. … When you line up over a guy, you’ve got to look him in his eye and say, ‘What’s my name? You’re going to respect me before this is all over.’”
#OnThisDay in 1967, Muhammad Ali delivered an iconic taunt against Ernie Terrell 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/KpRlquyCwq
— Top Rank Boxing (@trboxing) February 6, 2026
Giants tight end Chris Manhertz, a 10-year veteran, said the meeting room was stone-cold silent for a speech that lasted 10 to 15 minutes.
“For Coach Harbaugh to have his father address the team before his first game in a new organization shows how much respect he has for his father,” Manhertz told The Athletic .
“It definitely resonated with us. He had a lot of juice and energy for an 87-year-old man, and it was really about earning respect — not asking for it or begging for it — with your style of play. He’s a good storyteller, and he had us glued to our seats.”
And yes, this is why you hire John Harbaugh to coach your football team. He won 193 regular-season and postseason games over 18 years with the Baltimore Ravens because he knows how to motivate young people to do things they weren’t quite sure they could do.
This time around, Harbaugh correctly decided his father could be a useful source of inspiration. Hours before kickoff, the Giants coach pulled up to MetLife Stadium with his dad, his mother, Jackie, and his wife, Ingrid, among his passengers, all of them stunned by the masses already gathered in the parking lots.
“I was in awe of the tailgaters,” Harbaugh said in a quiet moment late Sunday night. “I couldn’t believe it. There are some big-ass NFL parking lots out there, and I’ve never seen one that full. There were people everywhere. And then the stadium was so freakin’ loud from the beginning to the end.”
Twenty-five years after the 9/11 attacks, Harbaugh’s old man was struck by a different sight as the family approached MetLife for the first night of the rest of their lives.
“What got me more was the New York skyline,” he said. “We were driving around this little corner, and you looked out and there was the skyline, and you realize just how close we were to the city. … It was 25 years ago and we can never forget what all those heroes did for us.”
The victims and the first responders were honored before the game. A moving ceremony gave way to football, and then the Giants went out there and made the Cowboys look small.
“I was so proud,” Jack Harbaugh said. “It wasn’t just a football game and a win. It was dominance. Just dominance.”
Back in the winter, when his son was deciding whether he should take the Giants job, Jack Harbaugh set John straight. Jack was an Ohio guy who loved telling stories about the battles waged between Cleveland’s Jim Brown and the Giants’ Sam Huff.
“That’s what football is all about,” Jack said. “And I told John one thing that might sound selfish or bad, but you have to consider where the Giants are and have been (historically) and where they should be in the NFL. ‘If you can go there and adjust that and put them in better position, what an accomplishment that would be for you and the city of New York.’”
John Harbaugh ultimately agreed. After the owner who hired him, Mara, gave him a game ball for his first Giants victory, the coach decided to award one to his father.
Harbaugh arrived in the locker room wearing a white “Never Forget” T-shirt. He looked drained for good reason. The whole experience of Game 1 in Year 1, he said, “was more than I expected, in all honesty. It was incredible. … It was really something, man.”
But Harbaugh still had enough energy left to complete his final task. He approached his father and reminded him that he never received a game ball for his 2002 national championship.
“We found the game ball,” John told Jack before handing it over to his dad. The son embraced his parents. The Giants coach said he was rewarding his old man “for what you did for our team motivation.”
It was John Harbaugh’s best call on a great night to be a New York Giant.

title: Jalen Hurts keeps 'meeting the moment' for Eagles to stay undefeated in season openers The offense was uneven in a 24-22 win over the Commanders, but Hurts knew how to take over and write his own script when necessary. Zach Berman 32

full_text:
Jalen Hurts is now the third quarterback since 1950 to win his first six season openers. Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — Jalen Hurts logged onto Zoom for a production meeting with Tom Brady on Saturday after the Philadelphia Eagles’ walkthrough. Chatting on a computer screen, the two Super Bowl MVPs discussed quarterbacking. Some of the conversation focused on the parts of the position that require no special talent: ensuring the team is in the right call with the right protection on a given play, or the type of mental requirements before the ball is even in his hands.
Those things are especially important in the first game with a new offensive coordinator and system. But there are moments when it doesn’t matter whether Hurts is under center or the receiver is in motion or what new concepts were implemented this summer. There are moments when the ball is in his hands and it’s up to him to take over.
“Yeah,” Hurts said after taking a few seconds to consider whether it’s true. “But it’s not something that’s forced.”
That’s what occurred in the Eagles’ 24-22 season-opening win over the Washington Commanders. Hurts finished 14 of 25 for 203 yards and three touchdowns. He also rushed for 46 yards. It was an uneven afternoon for the offense, which went three-and-out five times and failed to cross midfield on seven of their first nine drives. Yet the Eagles also totaled 318 yards and 6 yards per play, and they had five plays of 20-plus yards.
Most important, they won their sixth consecutive season opener in the Hurts/Nick Sirianni era and there were enough Hurts highlights to leave Eagles fans encouraged about what’s ahead.
For all the discussion about Hurts acclimating to this new offense and adding elements to his game that were not featured in previous systems, there were times when he leaned into areas in which he’s always excelled. He pinpointed a deep ball. He improvised with his legs. He made winning plays when they were needed.
“It’s just about meeting the moment when your opportunity comes,” Hurts said.
The most obvious example came in the fourth quarter. Washington had just narrowed the Eagles’ lead to 17-16, and the Eagles were backed up into a third-and-18.
“We should never be in … third-and-18,” Hurts said.
Hurts dropped back, hopped twice in the pocket and then tucked the ball and ran through a seam in the middle of the field for a 22-yard gain. On the broadcast, it was noted that Hurts figured he would “just do it myself.” It looked that way.
It was a moment when Hurts didn’t need to follow the script. He wrote his own.
“That’s probably the play of the game right there,” tight end Dallas Goedert said.
Two plays later, Goedert caught his second touchdown of the game. Goedert said Hurts killed the play late in the play clock, a testament to what Hurts observed before the snap that echoed part of his Saturday conversation with Brady. The Eagles took the eight-point lead they needed to win the game. It wouldn’t have happened without the scramble.
“It’s the beauty of having Jalen Hurts as your QB,” offensive tackle Jordan Mailata said. “He can make plays when plays are there.”
Or when the plays aren’t there.
The takeaway from Hurts’ performance was less about the consistent, down-to-down quarterbacking and more about the high-water marks. Hurts has been exceptional with the deep ball throughout his career. In the first half, he connected with Dontayvion Wicks on a 64-yard pass deep down the right sideline on a play that was apparently supposed to be a clearout route for the new receiver. Hurts recognized the matchup and placed the ball in a spot for Wicks to make a play.
“Jalen has worked extremely hard at that portion of his game,” Sirianni said. “He really can throw. He just puts the ball on the money in those situations, which helps you be explosive.”
Later in that drive, the Eagles scored their first touchdown when backed up on a third-and-goal at the 17. They ran a play that makes fans shudder: A version of the “four verts” that was the ill-fated final play in the playoffs last season, albeit against different coverage. This time, Hurts fit the ball into a tight window to Goedert at the perfect moment.
“Incredible job by Jalen, putting it high in the back of the end zone,” Goedert said. “Splitting like the red sea.”
Those highlights overshadowed the stalled drives, which marked much of offensive coordinator Sean Mannion’s debut . Part of the problem was ineffectiveness on first down that forced the Eagles to play behind the sticks. Their average distance to a first down on second down was 9.9 yards. Only the Miami Dolphins had a longer way to go among teams that have played in Week 1. The Eagles are tied for the highest three-and-out percentage in the NFL this weekend thus far. But they also did not turn the ball over, and 9.4 percent of their plays resulted in gains of 20-plus yards — a better percentage than all but one game last season.
“I thought he did a good job of getting the play in. The operation’s the first thing you always look at,” Sirianni said of Mannion. “I thought we were pretty balanced in our situations of the way we kind of break it down. I thought we were able to be explosive. We would’ve liked to finish the third one in the red zone because those are always big, but we were two-for-three in the red zone. Even in some tough situations, we got behind the sticks in the red zone on both of our first two scores, and I thought he did a good job calling it on that one to try to get us back.”
There’s a survive-and-advance element to season openers. The Commanders had a first-time coordinator and new personnel. Teams are trying to learn themselves, not to mention their opponents. The blocking must improve. The run game must avoid negative plays. There were also misfired passes by Hurts.
Knowing this, you seek what sticks. That’s why Hurts’ performance should not be dismissed. The two big scrambles (23 yards and 14 yards), the deep ball to Wicks (as well as a fadeaway touchdown pass to him), the tight-window passes to Goedert and DeVonta Smith are all moments that can carry over. Further, they were evidence of times when Hurts can take over the game when the moment calls for it. It’s happened before with Hurts. It will happen again.
Hurts is now the third quarterback since 1950 to win his first six season openers, joining Hall of Famers Roger Staubach and Johnny Unitas. Sirianni reviewed those wins this week in search of trends. He noticed that Hurts has made plays with his legs in those games, too. In fact, Hurts averages 55 rushing yards per game in season openers — nearly 14 yards more per game than his average in all other weeks.
“I think one of the things that makes Jalen such a special quarterback,” Sirianni said, “is that he can do it through the air. He can do it running the show. He can do it with his legs when he needs to make plays, and obviously, that was a big play, and you need those.”
It’s a good reminder about the quarterback who once called him a “triple-threat.” There’s so much to the position that he discussed with Brady that only quarterbacks can understand. There are parts of his game under scrutiny in the new offense. But there are times when the Eagles must trust that their franchise quarterback will make a play in ways that defy explanation, that somebody who defines himself by winning will make the winning plays.
“It’s just playing ball,” Hurts said while considering more details before smiling and nodding his head.  “Going out there and playing ball, yeah.”

full_text:
The Seahawks picked off Patriots QB Drake Maye three times in the fourth quarter of their season-opening win. Jane Gershovich / Getty Images
With just 26 seconds remaining in Wednesday night’s season opener against the New England Patriots, star Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba held his breath, hoping desperately that Seattle’s defense would step up.
As it often did during the Seahawks’ Super Bowl run, the unit that calls itself the Dark Side rose to the occasion. Cornerback Josh Jobe picked off Patriots quarterback Drake Maye, one of three fourth-quarter interceptions for the Seahawks, as they overcame a 10-point deficit and held on for a 13-10 win.
“We can always count on our defense, best defense in the league,” Smith-Njigba said postgame. “Just hard-nosed and super happy for Jobe. I was happy to see him go attack the ball and keep his feet in and look like a receiver right there.”
Jobe was hardly the only defensive back to stand out on a night when the Seahawks were short a few of them. Nickelback Nick Emmanwori, who had ankle surgery in July, sat out. So did safety Ty Okada, who is sidelined with a hamstring injury, and it’s unclear how long he will be sidelined, according to coach Mike Macdonald.
With Emmanwori and Okada unavailable, Seattle inserted safety Rodney Thomas II, who was elevated from the practice squad for Wednesday’s game, into the starting lineup. Thomas demonstrated why he was once a regular starter, doing so for 26 games over the last four seasons with the Indianapolis Colts.
The 28-year-old delivered a pair of stellar plays, both of which Macdonald commended him on. On second-and-12 with under nine minutes to go in the third quarter, Thomas was all over a swing pass to New England’s DeMario Douglas, holding the wide receiver to a 1-yard gain en route to Seattle forcing a three-and-out.
“The play he made in the flat on one of (Devon Witherspoon’s) pressures was a tremendous play,” Macdonald said. “Making an open-field tackle, running out of the post on a hot throw in the flat for, like, a no-yard gain. That’s something he’s been working on, and it shows you that if you put intent behind areas of improvement, you can make all that stuff come to life.”
Perhaps more importantly, Thomas paved the way for Seattle’s first interception. When Maye took a shot down the left sideline for wide receiver Romeo Doubs with 14:27 to go in the fourth quarter, Thomas timed his pass breakup perfectly.
The deflected ball popped straight in the air and neatly settled into cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett’s hands. Thomas finished the evening with four tackles and one pass defensed, much to Macdonald’s excitement.
“He should be proud of himself,” Macdonald said. “But it’s just the beginning.”
Seattle’s performance without a few key defensive backs stood in stark contrast to a season ago.
The NFL’s top-scoring defense was without both Witherspoon and Julian Love on Oct. 5, 2025, against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, while Emmanwori was just returning after an injury in the season opener. Quarterback Baker Mayfield torched Seattle’s secondary for 379 passing yards and 38 points, the most the Seahawks gave up in a game last season, in a 38-35 win for the Buccaneers.
Though Emmanwori’s absence was still felt on Wednesday, the rest of Seattle’s secondary — familiar and unfamiliar names alike — delivered in a dominating way. In between Pritchett’s and Jobe’s interceptions was one by Love, who jumped a pass intended for Douglas on third-and-14 with 9:25 to go in the fourth quarter.
Love, who is in his fourth season with the Seahawks but was limited to eight games last year because of a hamstring injury, had six tackles (two for loss) and a pass deflection.
“Julian Love played his best game as a Seahawk,” Macdonald said, “and that’s saying something.”
Aside from Love, Macdonald was also pleased with Pritchett, who was tied for the third-most tackles (six) on the team versus New England. Linebacker Ernest Jones IV led the way with 13 tackles, while Drake Thomas wasn’t far behind with nine.
Pritchett appeared in all 17 regular-season games for Seattle last year, yet he wasn’t much of a tackler, logging 14 in total. His coverage on the outside was solid against Patriots wide receivers like Mack Hollins and A.J. Brown. But what impressed Macdonald most was that Pritchett wasn’t afraid to join his fellow defensive backs in lowering his shoulder when necessary.
“He had some great tackles,” Macdonald said. “Our whole secondary did.”
“It’s beautiful to see one of the young guys step up and command his role like Nehemiah,” added veteran edge rusher DeMarcus Lawrence. “He’s definitely going to be a star in this league.”
Seattle’s secondary might look a bit different soon. Emmanwori has recently returned to the practice field and continues to inch closer to game action. Once he’s cleared to play, Thomas could head back to the bench.
Rookie cornerback Avery Smith, whom the Seahawks acquired from the Los Angeles Chargers on Aug. 30 for a 2027 sixth-round pick, did not play Wednesday. Neither did two-time Pro Bowl cornerback Trevon Diggs, who signed a one-year deal on Aug. 19 but is on Seattle’s practice squad as he gets up to speed.
Defensive coordinator Aden Durde said he thinks Diggs, 28 on Sunday, has a solid enough grasp of Seattle’s playbook to take the field. Macdonald declined to say whether Diggs is close to being added to the 53-man roster.
“We’ll see. He’s doing a great job, though,” Macdonald said. “He’s been awesome. Great guy, buying into how we do things here, and an awesome guy to be around. The guys love him, so we’re excited to have him.”
Whether Diggs or Smith becomes an impactful player in 2026, let alone sees the gridiron that often, will be determined in time. But Seattle’s secondary, which was subject to ample concerns last month when rookie safety Bud Clark went down with a season-ending ankle injury, proved in its first showing of the season it has plenty of quality depth to work with, despite the offseason departures of Coby Bryant and Riq Woolen.
Rookie third-round pick Julian Neal, who sat out most of training camp with a quad injury but was active Wednesday, did not play a snap on defense. When Emmanwori and Okada return, and Neal is fully healthy, it will only bolster a defense that was perhaps the NFL’s best in 2025 and could be even stronger in 2026.
The defensive backs who were on the field Wednesday, such as Jobe, were unfazed when the game’s outcome was in jeopardy. In the process, Seattle nailed its first test.
“We live in the death zone, and we came alive, and we took the ball away,” Jobe said of his interception. “That’s what we talked about throughout the week: take the ball away and keep our eye on the ball.”

full_text:
The San Francisco 49ers had some tricks up their sleeve that helped give the running game, including rookie Kaelon Black, an edge. Kirby Lee / IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect
We were all guilty of worrying about the San Francisco 49ers’ apparent hole at left guard, and how the offensive line as a whole would fare against the super team that is the Los Angeles Rams.
Silly us. 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan has always had his buddy Sean McVay’s number, and the Rams and their coach might not have been ready for the 49ers’ use of motion in the running game even if they weren’t jet-lagged. The 49ers ran for 174 yards in the 27-7 win , using pre-snap movement to get better angles and win the edges.
The 49ers featured motion at the snap on 65 percent of their offensive plays, the highest rate in a game since Shanahan took over as coach in 2017, per NFL Next Gen Stats. They gained 251 of their 379 total yards on those plays.
“Our coaches and their game plan, and our tight ends, fullbacks, running backs, wide receivers on the chips kept their edges out of it,” tight end George Kittle said. “Yeah, football is a really hard sport, and it doesn’t honestly matter who you have lined up — you still have to go out there and execute every single snap. And our O-line and all the guys who were part of (run) blocking, I think they did an excellent job.”
Kittle, and especially fullback Kyle Juszczyk, used quick motion on the wing to slow the Rams’ pass rush and get them leaning the wrong way. The 49ers often used double movement (a shift, then motion) to free up running backs Christian McCaffrey and Kaelon Black.
McCaffrey dealt with cramps in the first half and finished with 10 carries for 68 yards, while the rookie Black showed his thirst for contact and speed with 14 carries for 65 yards. Last season, no 49ers running back other than McCaffrey had more than nine carries in one game.
Deebo Samuel added a 12-yard run. The 49ers’ 5.8 yards per carry and 0.19 EPA per carry would have been season-bests a year ago.
Black “did incredible,” McCaffrey said. “Oh, he’s an awesome back, man. I said this earlier, but he’s a force, and he’s someone who’s going to help our team a whole lot.”
Now, did McCaffrey and Black get a borderline illegal boost from Juszczyk? That’s up for debate.
The fullback was in motion at the snap on more than half of his snaps (17 of 33), and he wasn’t always moving horizontally . He would go backward, and then time his turn upfield with the snap to give him a running start into blocks against flat-footed defenders.
Future Hall of Fame defensive end and current CBS analyst J.J. Watt wrote on social media that he will be “interested to see if the league cracks down” on these “banana shaped motions.”
To which Juszczyk replied, “Let’s not draw attention to this,” with a “shh” emoji.
The rulebook states that an offensive player cannot be moving toward the line of scrimmage at the snap, but lateral motion is permitted. The 49ers’ motions are carefully coordinated with these rules in mind.
In any case, the season-opening win definitely drew attention to the 49ers’ offense, and Black should continue to have a bigger role as the Niners return home from Australia to host league doormats Miami and Arizona. Shanahan promises to reduce McCaffrey’s workload every offseason. But he appears to mean it this year, and the rookie out of Indiana now seems like a value pick as a third-rounder, despite many criticizing the pick as a reach after it happened.
It turns out Shanahan had some tricks up his sleeve as well.

full_text:
Stefon Diggs was penalized for his celebration after scoring a fourth-quarter touchdown for the Washington Commanders. Mitchell Leff / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — By the time Stefon Diggs hauled in a 10-yard pass from Jayden Daniels and leaped into the end zone at Lincoln Financial Field, Sunday had been a largely frustrating day for the Washington Commanders’ offense.
“Finally, we hit one, and I get a little excited,” Diggs said of the score that pulled Washington within 17-15 of the Philadelphia Eagles with 9:59 remaining in the game.
Diggs, though, immediately granted the Eagles a gift. He ran through the end zone and bear-hugged the goal post.
A penalty flag flew immediately: unsportsmanlike conduct. Instead of potentially going for a game-tying two-point conversion — which Washington coach Dan Quinn said he would have attempted — the Commanders were pushed back 15 yards, and Drew Stevens’ extra-point attempt came from 48 yards. (He made it to pull the Commanders within one.)
“Just got to be smarter, you know,” Daniels said. “You got to know the situation, situational football. … There’s a time and place for everything in celebrations.”
After the Eagles scored a touchdown and added an extra point to push their lead back to 8, the Commanders reached the end zone again with about a minute left. A failed two-point try left the Eagles ahead 24-22, which was the final score .
Goal posts have been off-limits for celebrations dating to the days when New Orleans Saints tight end Jimmy Graham used to dunk footballs over the crossbar — right as Diggs was entering the league in 2015. The veteran receiver, who joined the Commanders as a free agent in August, was contrite.
“Of course, I take full accountability,” Diggs said. “And I want to win bad, you know — every little rep, everything. So finally when we clicked after not clicking for a little while, it got to me a little.”
Given how NFL players celebrate these days, getting assessed 15 yards for hugging the goal post might seem extreme. Diggs didn’t show anybody up, nor did he damage any equipment. Entire defenses sprint the length of the field to mug for the television cameras after turnovers. But Diggs said he knew the rules.
“As soon as I wrapped my arms around it, I was like, ‘Oh, I forgot,'” he said. “It’s not back in the day. We’ve been playing for a long time. You used to do that. … That’s just telling me I’ve been in the game a long time. You’re like, ‘I got to be better.'”

full_text:
Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles made several splash plays for the Commanders in his debut, including this sack of Jalen Hurts. Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — The seven-word message became the Washington Commanders’ game-day creed in 2024 and has hung around ever since — literally. “WE WILL OUT HIT EVERY TEAM WE PLAY,” written in block letters and surrounded by the signatures of Commanders players, is stamped on a small sign that always hangs inside Washington’s locker room, at home and on the road.
From city to city, the sign followed the team through its deep playoff run two years ago and its steep fall in 2025, constantly reminding of the identity Washington has been trying to build.
On Sunday, in the Commanders’ 24-22 season-opening loss to the Philadelphia Eagles, that creed became the crux of a defense that showed marked improvement from last season, but that has plenty of work ahead.
“I think we showed that we’re good enough to beat them,” cornerback Rasul Douglas said. “We just didn’t. But (Daronte) called a great game plan, and I think we know what is required.”
The Commanders’ opener displayed the beginnings of what the team hopes will be a season-long progression for its defense under first-year coordinator Daronte Jones. The longtime defensive backs coach, who came to Washington from Minnesota, was tabbed to overhaul a unit that was a liability in numerous games over the last two years thanks to a stagnant pass rush and leaky secondary.
Jones’ system is multiple but predicated largely on Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ high-press scheme, with plenty of pre-snap disguises, overloaded fronts and interchangeable assignments.
Facing Philadelphia’s vaunted offensive line and its multiple playmakers, Washington held the Eagles to only 10 first downs, half as many as the Commanders’ offense. That was the lowest total in the league through the first 15 games of Week 1.
The physicality coach Dan Quinn has preached since he arrived in Washington two seasons ago was evident throughout, with 13 total “havoc” plays — takeaways, tackles for loss, sacks and pass breakups — the Commanders’ fourth-most in a game since the start of the ’24 season.
Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles, who wore the green dot in the second half when Frankie Luvu was sidelined with a groin injury, showed his mettle in the third quarter when he trucked Eagles running back Saquon Barkley on the way to his first career sack. On the next drive, he stuffed Barkley for a three-yard loss on a run.
Just as promising as the production was much of Washington’s process: It sent five-man pressures on 12 of the Eagles’ 33 dropbacks and generated pressure on two-thirds of them.
The Commanders’ defense was a primary reason the game stayed close when the offense struggled to find a rhythm. But there were still costly miscues — and such mistakes could cost the Commanders much more this season if the defense can’t eliminate them.
“Those are the ones that can change field position and make such a big difference,” Quinn said, adding, “I like our speed, I like our hitting, I like our physicality, I like being in and out of pressure for us, but let’s (eliminate) these explosive plays as best we can. … There were too many of them tonight.”
The Commanders gave up seven explosive plays, all of which either helped set up Eagles scores or were the scores themselves.
The first was a 64-yard catch by Dontayvion Wicks with just under two minutes left in the opening quarter. After coming up with stops on third-and-longs in each of the Eagles’ first two series — Douglas had a pass-breakup on a third-and-8 and Luvu had a nine-yard sack of Jalen Hurts on a third-and-12 — Washington let the Eagles flip the field on a busted coverage. Three plays later, Hurts connected with tight end Dallas Goedert on a 17-yard touchdown pass.
Later in the second quarter, Barkley manufactured a long run when Commanders cornerback Amik Robertson and linebacker Leo Chenal collided as they converged near the line of scrimmage. Barkley cut to the right to dodge Mike Sainristil and slipped past safety Jeremy Reaves to pick up 42 yards. Hurts found Wicks for a touchdown two plays later.
The costliest mistake, though, was on a 22-yard scramble by Hurts on third-and-18 in the fourth quarter. Washington’s offense had started to find a rhythm and had just trimmed the Eagles’ lead to 17-16.
“That third-and-18 play was killer,” outside linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson said. “That’s something as the D-line, we got to make sure we manage that and have control of that.”
The Commanders had wanted to go for two after Stefon Diggs’ touchdown catch on the previous series, which would have tied the score if successful, but an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty against Diggs for bear-hugging the goalpost forced them to settle for an extra point.
A defensive stop would have put the Commanders in position to try to claim the lead. Instead, their defense let Hurts sprint through a wide gap in the middle of the line for a first down.
Three plays later, after the Commanders loaded the line of scrimmage to disguise pressure, they gave up a 43-yard touchdown. Styles and outside linebacker Odafe Oweh both seemed to think Goedert jumped forward before the snap. But the officials didn’t call anything, and Goedert turned a short catch on a slant into the game-winning score.
“On that one, there’s a lesson for us too, whether it was or was not (a false start): We still have to finish,” Quinn said.
“We gotta come out faster,” Douglas said. “Can’t get punched in the mouth, but then want to fight. When somebody tells you they’re gonna fight you all day at school, when you see them, you gotta go punch them. You can’t just wait. … We didn’t start fast, and we didn’t do what we’re supposed to do.”

full_text:
Jayden Daniels made it through Washington's Week 1 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles upright and lamenting missed opportunities. Bill Streicher / Imagn Images
“We had frustrations throughout the game,” Washington Commanders receiver Stefon Diggs said after the Philadelphia Eagles’ 24-22 win Sunday. “Finally, we get one, and I get a little overzealous, I get a little excited. Of course I take responsibility.”
Diggs’ unsportsmanlike conduct penalty after his 10-yard touchdown catch from Jayden Daniels with 10 minutes left in the game was the biggest miscue in Washington’s loss. There were, though, others. After Daniels’ 1-yard scoring pass to rookie Antonio Williams with 1:01 left, Washington attempted a 2-point conversion to tie it. But Philly defensive tackle Moro Ojomo blew up David Blough’s play — a shovel pass from Daniels to tight end John Bates — by beating a double-team block by center Nick Allegretti and right tackle Josh Conerly Jr., and stopped Bates short of the goal line.
Washington’s offense showed some good things at the Linc, but there were too many mistakes to beat a beatable Eagles team in the regular-season opener. Diggs’ was the most obvious; a vet can’t do that, even though the league’s rules on what you can and can’t do in celebration are kind of inconsistent. ( You can hide behind the goal post , for example, but you can’t hug it.)
Everything matters along the margins, and especially in divisional games. Now the Commanders are behind the eight ball a week into the season, with as close to a must-win — on the road, again, against an NFC East foe, again — at the Dallas Cowboys next week.
Teachable moments are important, to be sure, for a team’s growth. But road dubs count for more when everything gets added up at season’s end.
For most of the first three quarters, the Commanders offense, and Blough, its first-year offensive coordinator , got very little done, wasting multiple opportunities given to it by Washington’s defense, which stacked three-and-outs much of the night and forced seven Eagles punts. (To be sure: The defense gave up a handful of killer big plays, too.) Washington’s offense produced a field goal on its first possession, then didn’t move the ball again until its next-to-last possession of the first half. Eagles linebacker Zack Baun was just … everywhere.
Sunday marked the first time Daniels started and finished a game for Washington since Oct. 13, against the Chicago Bears. Think of that: It’s almost been a year since Jayden Daniels actually played four full quarters for the Commanders. That is a significant hurdle for him to overcome, after his disastrous 2025, which included separate hamstring, knee and elbow injuries that limited him to seven games. He is the North Star for owner Josh Harris’ team, capable of doing great things when on the field. With Daniels, Washington has a chance.
He wasn’t dropping dimes in buckets 60 yards downfield Sunday. He wasn’t whirling around the field, play after play, with the ball in his hands. He ran when he had to. But he didn’t take off at the first sign of trouble.
“It’s great to have Jayden back,” Dan Quinn said.
“I thought that was significant. It was good to see him also learn some lessons from ’25 — making a play, get down, throw the ball away. Those are things that, as a coach, I don’t really know until we get into the games. He’s such a competitor. I thought, man, it’s good to have him back into this space.”
Daniels, in his third season, looked like a quarterback who understood his importance. He didn’t take off at the first sign of pressure. He tried to climb the pocket and throw downfield, and when that wasn’t available, he threw the ball away. He ran Blough’s plays well, and spread the ball around. The Eagles played cloud coverage with safety help on Terry McLaurin most of the day, so Daniels went to Williams, Diggs and Chig Okonkwo. Washington wants to get McLaurin 10 targets a game. He had four Sunday.
It took Daniels and the offense a while to get going, but the Commanders scored touchdowns on both of their fourth-quarter possessions. Bill Croskey-Merritt and rookie Kaytron Allen had good interior runs (and BCM was bailed out when Conerly recovered his fumble on the last drive, at the Eagles’ 19), as Washington averaged better than 4 yards a carry against the Eagles’ stout front. Williams had four catches for 64 yards in his NFL debut.
“We stopped shooting ourselves in the foot, being in third-and-longs, especially against a really good defense like that, and especially away,” said Daniels, who was 18-of-34 for 164 yards and two touchdowns. “You don’t want to play in third-and-longs and let that crowd and that defense feast and rally to the ball. We shot ourselves in the foot too many times. … Obviously, the loss sucks. You don’t want to come out here and lose. Credit to Philly. But, God bless, I’m just happy to be out here playing football again.”
As the game went on, the offensive line gave Daniels more time. The backs did an excellent job, for the most part, in blitz pickups, and Daniels started getting the ball downfield.
“I don’t think it’s really about clicking; you just have to keep going,” left tackle Brandon Coleman said. “You have to trust, in everything. We have huge amounts of trust in Blough; he has huge amounts of trust in us. So just making sure that we played to the standard we’re supposed to.”
Daniels had an option, on the 2-point attempt, to pull the ball back before the shovel pass and go to running back Rachaad White in the flat. If he had done so, White was wide open. But Daniels stuck with the initial read.
“It was an option, but I’ve got to do my job, too,” Daniels said. “The defensive end played up the field. We had the look that we wanted. We just didn’t execute.”
The Commanders won’t likely be able to repeat the magical season Daniels and the offense had in 2024, when the Commanders unleashed him upon the league. They play more deliberately now, and don’t want him taking off as much. The new plan, which must work for anything else to matter, is to play games such as Sunday’s, where the offense might take a while to get in sync before clicking, and where the defense and special teams will have to carry more of the load, at least early on. It’s not as electrifying, but if it gives Daniels a better chance to stay in one piece game after game, season after season, the Commanders will take the tradeoff.

title: Josh Sweat Had Perfect Response to Noisy Cardinals Offseason
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals OLB Josh Sweat heard the noise this offseason.
Sweat, heavily involved in trade chatter, ultimately wasn't moved by the Cardinals before the 2026 season. Many believed the pass rusher was disgruntled after Arizona fired head coach Jonathan Gannon, and reports indicated teams were calling on Sweat before training camp.
Nothing transpired. Sweat remained on PUP after having a procedure done but was taken off the list ahead of the regular season. Sweat played 53% of snaps in the season opener, the most of any outside linebacker. He tallied two tackles (one for loss) in the upset win over the Los Angeles Chargers.
After the game, Sweat spoke with AZCardinals.com's Zach Gershman and addressed the entire offseason that made him a prominent headline and talking point.
"There was a lot of noise in the offseason, but I didn't respond purposely," said Sweat . "I just wanted to see how far people's imagination could take it."
Sweat notably was thought to be a potential trade candidate to land with the Green Bay Packers, given their need for a pass rusher and connection with Gannon — who is now their defensive coordinator.
That didn't come to fruition, and after so much talk about Sweat being unhappy with the Cardinals, the pass rusher set the record straight.
"People think I only came here for one reason and that was Jonathan Gannon, and yeah, that made the decision easier for me, but I know the guys that were here," Sweat added.
"I love the way they play. I love that we want to make something bigger happen here. It's too good of a place to be where it was last year.
The Cardinals certainly need Sweat to repeat his 12-sack output from last season if they'll continue to shock the world moving into the depths of the season. Perhaps familiarity with defensive coordinator Nick Rallis and his scheme will help moving forward as well.
There's no doubting Sweat's ability to get after the quarterback while freeing up opportunities for his fellow defenders. There's also no doubting Arizona's defense is reliant on Sweat to consistently do what he does best.
At least for now, trade rumors will die down. Perhaps around the November deadline they'll pick back up again.
Yet Sweat insists he's exactly where he wants to be. And if you ask anyone on the Cardinals, they'd say the same exact thing.
